What are End-to-End ML Projects? 
End-to-end Machine Learning (ML) projects involve the complete workflow of developing and deploying a machine learning model, encompassing every stage from problem definition to model deployment. These projects provide a comprehensive learning experience by covering all essential aspects of the ML pipeline. 
Why are End-to-End ML Projects Needed? 
End-to-end ML projects are essential because they: 
Provide Comprehensive Learning: Cover the entire ML lifecycle from data collection to model deployment. 
Develop Essential Skills: Enhance technical, problem-solving, and project management skills. 
Create Real-World Solutions: Enable the deployment of models for real-time predictions and continuous updates. 
Build Strong Portfolios: Showcase expertise and versatility to potential employers or clients. 
Align with Business Goals: Ensure models meet business objectives and provide measurable impact. 
Now, let’s delve into the project we’re building, which is Toxic Comment Detection. In Part I, we’ll focus on notebook experimentation. 
PART-I

Anyway, let’s move on. 
Transformation of Data # Convert True to 1 and False to 0 in the 'Toxic' column df[ 'Toxic' ] = df[ 'Toxic' ].astype( int ) def clean_text ( text ): text = text.lower() text = re.sub( r"what's" , "what is " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'s" , " " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'ve" , " have " , text) text = re.sub( r"can't" , "cannot " , text) text = re.sub( r"n't" , " not " , text) text = re.sub( r"i'm" , "i am " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'re" , " are " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'d" , " would " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'ll" , " will " , text) text = re.sub( r"\'scuse" , " excuse " , text) text = re.sub( '\W' , ' ' , text) text = re.sub( '\s+' , ' ' , text) text = text.strip( ' ' ) return text # clean the comment_text in train_df [Thanks to Pulkit Jha for the useful pointer.] df[ 'Text' ] = df[ 'Text' ]. map ( lambda com : clean_text(com)) Now that the data is cleaned, bathed, and ready for the vectorizer. 
NERD: What is a vectorizer and why are we using it? 
A vectorizer, specifically a TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) vectorizer in this context, plays a crucial role in natural language processing (NLP) and text analysis tasks. Let’s break down what a vectorizer is and why we use it: 
What is a Vectorizer? 
Text to Numerical Conversion: A vectorizer converts text data into numerical vectors that machine learning algorithms can process. In NLP, algorithms typically work with numerical data, so we need to transform textual information into a format that the algorithms can understand. 
Feature Extraction: Vectorizers extract features from text by representing words or phrases as numerical values. These features capture important information about the text, such as word frequency, relevance, and context. 
Dimensionality Reduction: They can help reduce the dimensionality of the text data by creating sparse matrices where each row represents a document or text sample, and each column represents a unique word or term in the corpus. 
Why Use Vectorizers? 
Input Format for Machine Learning Models: Machine learning models, especially those used for text classification or sentiment analysis, require numerical input. Vectorizers enable us to convert raw text data into a format that these models can process and learn from. 
Feature Representation: Vectorizers capture semantic information from text, such as word importance and relationships between words. This allows machine learning models to learn patterns and make predictions based on the features extracted from the text. 
Efficient Data Representation: They provide an efficient and compact representation of text data, especially in high-dimensional spaces where the number of unique words or features can be large. This efficiency is crucial for training and deploying machine learning models effectively. 
Normalization and Scaling: Vectorizers often perform normalization and scaling of the numerical values, which can improve the performance and stability of machine learning algorithms, especially when dealing with diverse text data. 
Handling Sparse Data: Text data is often sparse, meaning that most words or features in a document are zero or absent. Vectorizers handle sparse data efficiently, storing only non-zero values and saving memory and computational resources. 
Phew! Now that the “boring” stuff is over, let’s dive into the coding part. 
# Vectorize the text data using TF-IDF vect = TfidfVectorizer(max_features= 5000 , stop_words= 'english' ) X = vect.fit_transform(df[ 'Text' ]) Y = df[ 'Toxic' ] Toxic-comments (Personified): You promised you would provide us Justice!!! Yes, yes, I did promise, didn’t I? Let’s do it then. My trusted SMOTE will help you with this. Let’s get going. Ahhh, this nerd is back again. 
NERD: What is SMOTE? 
SMOTE stands for Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. It’s a technique used in machine learning, specifically in dealing with imbalanced datasets, where one class (the minority class) is significantly underrepresented compared to another class (the majority class). Here’s a breakdown of what SMOTE is: 
Addressing Class Imbalance: SMOTE is designed to address the problem of class imbalance in datasets, where one class (usually the minority class) has far fewer samples than the other class (the majority class). This imbalance can lead to biased models that perform poorly on the minority class. 
Generating Synthetic Samples: SMOTE works by generating synthetic samples for the minority class. It does this by creating new instances (or synthetic samples) that are combinations of the existing minority class samples. These synthetic samples are created by interpolating between existing minority class samples in the feature space. 
Interpolation Technique: SMOTE selects pairs of similar instances from the minority class and creates synthetic instances along the line segments joining these pairs. This process effectively increases the number of samples in the minority class, making it more balanced with the majority class. 
Maintaining Data Distribution: The synthetic samples generated by SMOTE are created in a way that maintains the distribution and patterns of the minority class, thereby preventing overfitting and improving the generalization of the machine learning model. 
Now that the NERD is satisfied, let’s get back on track 
# Import SMOTE from imblearn from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE # Initialize SMOTE smote = SMOTE() # Apply SMOTE for oversampling X_resampled, y_resampled = smote.fit_resample(X, Y)\ # Convert the oversampled data back to a DataFrame df_resampled = pd.DataFrame(X_resampled.todense(), columns=vect.get_feature_names_out()) df_resampled[ 'Toxic' ] = y_resampled # Check the distribution after oversampling toxic_distribution_after = df_resampled[ 'Toxic' ].value_counts() print ( "\nDistribution after SMOTE:" ) print (toxic_distribution_after) # Bar plot for toxic vs non-toxic comments plt.figure(figsize=( 8 , 6 )) toxic_counts = df_resampled[ 'Toxic' ].value_counts() toxic_counts.plot(kind= 'bar' , color=[ 'green' , 'red' ]) plt.title( 'Toxic vs Non-Toxic Comments' ) plt.xlabel( 'Toxic' ) plt.ylabel( 'Count' ) plt.xticks(rotation= 0 ) plt.show() Now that justice is served, let’s split the data for model building. The data is ready for modeling, so let’s build the model. 
# Split the resampled data into training and testing sets x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_resampled, y_resampled, test_size= 0.2 , random_state= 42 ) # Build the neural network model with Input layer model = Sequential([ Dense( 64 , activation= 'relu' ), Dropout( 0.5 ), Dense( 1 , activation= 'sigmoid' ) ]) # Compile the model model. compile (optimizer=Adam(learning_rate= 0.001 ), loss= 'binary_crossentropy' , metrics=[ 'accuracy' ]) A simple neural network with very few neurons ensures that the model is lightweight, and using a dropout of 0.5 helps prevent overfitting. 
Now, let’s train the model. 
# Train the model history = model.fit(x_train.toarray(), y_train, epochs= 10 , batch_size= 32 , validatio n_split= 0.2 ) import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Plot training & validation accuracy values plt.figure(figsize=( 10 , 6 )) plt.plot(history.history[ 'accuracy' ]) plt.plot(history.history[ 'val_accuracy' ]) plt.title( 'Model Accuracy' ) plt.xlabel( 'Epoch' ) plt.ylabel( 'Accuracy' ) plt.legend([ 'Train' , 'Validation' ], loc= 'upper left' ) plt.show() # Plot training & validation loss values plt.figure(figsize=( 10 , 6 )) plt.plot(history.history[ 'loss' ]) plt.plot(history.history[ 'val_loss' ]) plt.title( 'Model Loss' ) plt.xlabel( 'Epoch' ) plt.ylabel( 'Loss' ) plt.legend([ 'Train' , 'Validation' ], loc= 'upper left' ) plt.show() Now that’s Great! But let’s ensure that the model is not overfitting. Moving on to model evaluation, we can confirm that the model is not overfitting. 
# Evaluate the model on the test set loss, accuracy = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test) print ( f'Test Accuracy: {accuracy} ' ) # Generate predictions on the test set y_pred_proba = model.predict(x_test) y_pred = (y_pred_proba > 0.5 ).astype( int ) # Generate classification report report = classification_report(y_test, y_pred) print (report) # Generate predictions on the test set y_pred_proba = model.predict(x_test) y_pred = (y_pred_proba > 0.5 ).astype( int ) # Generate classification report report = classification_report(y_test, y_pred, output_dict= True ) df_report = pd.DataFrame(report).transpose() # Extract relevant metrics for visualization class_metrics = df_report.drop([ 'accuracy' , 'macro avg' , 'weighted avg' ]) # Plotting the classification report metrics using a heatmap plt.figure(figsize=( 8 , 6 )) sns.heatmap(class_metrics[[ 'precision' , 'recall' , 'f1-score' ]], annot= True , cmap= 'coolwarm' , fmt= ".2f" ) plt.title( 'Classification Report Metrics' ) plt.xlabel( 'Metrics' ) plt.ylabel( 'Class' ) plt.yticks(rotation= 0 ) plt.show() now that we know model is not overfitting . 
Next, let’s save the vectorizer and model for further use locally. Here’s the code for using the saved model and vectorizer 
import pickle with open ( 'tfidf_vectorizer.pkl' , 'wb' ) as f: pickle.dump(vect, f) # Save Keras model model.save( 'toxic_comment_model.h5' ) Usage Code(using saved Model and Vectorizer)

Template Creation 
NERD: Why is a template required? 
A template is essential because it ensures uniformity across all projects and reduces the manual effort needed to create folders and files each time you start a new project. With a template, you can maintain a proper structure and uniformity throughout all your end-to-end projects. 
You need only one file, template.py , to serve as the template for all your projects from now on. 
template.py 
import os from pathlib import Path import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format = '[%(asctime)s]:%(message)s:' ) project_name = "Toxic_comment_detection" list_of_files =[ ".github/workflows/.gitkeep" , f"src/ {project_name} /__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /components/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /utils/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /utils/common.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /config/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /config/configuration.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /pipeline/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /entity/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /entity/config_entity.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /constants/__init__.py" , "config/config.yaml" , "params.yaml" , "schema.yaml" , "main.py" , "app.py" , "Dockerfile" , "requirements.txt" , "setup.py" , "research/trials.ipynb" , "templates/index.html" , ] for filepath in list_of_files: filepath = Path(filepath) filedir, filename = os.path.split(filepath) if filedir != "" : os.makedirs(filedir, exist_ok= True ) logging.info( f"Creating directory; {filedir} for the file: {filename} " ) if ( not os.path.exists(filepath)) or (os.path.getsize(filepath) == 0 ): with open (filepath, "w" ) as f: pass logging.info( f"Creating empty file: {filepath} " ) else : logging.info( f" {filename} is already exists" ) Detailed Explanation of template.py(Skip if you don’t think its needed) 
import os from pathlib import Path import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format = '[%(asctime)s]: %(message)s:' ) Import Statements : 
os : This module provides a way of using operating system-dependent functionality like reading or writing to the file system. 
Path from pathlib : This module offers classes representing filesystem paths with semantics appropriate for different operating systems. 
logging : This module is used to set up a logging system that allows you to report status, error, and informational messages. 
2. Logging Configuration : 
logging.basicConfig(...) : This sets up the logging configuration with a specified log level ( INFO ) and a format for log messages. The format includes the timestamp and the message. 
project_name = "Toxic_comment_detection" 3. Project Name : 
project_name : This variable holds the name of the project, which is used in various file paths to maintain a consistent project structure. 
list_of_files = [ ".github/workflows/.gitkeep" , f"src/ {project_name} /__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /components/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /utils/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /utils/common.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /config/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /config/configuration.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /pipeline/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /entity/__init__.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /entity/config_entity.py" , f"src/ {project_name} /constants/__init__.py" , "config/config.yaml" , "params.yaml" , "schema.yaml" , "main.py" , "app.py" , "Dockerfile" , "requirements.txt" , "setup.py" , "research/trials.ipynb" , "templates/index.html" , ] 4. List of Files : 
list_of_files : This list contains the relative paths of all the files and directories that need to be created for the project. Each path is specified as a string, and some use the project_name variable to maintain consistency in the project structure. 
for filepath in list_of_files: filepath = Path (filepath) filedir, filename = os.path. split (filepath) if filedir != "" : os. makedirs (filedir, exist_ok=True) logging. info (f "Creating directory: {filedir} for the file: {filename}" ) 5. File and Directory Creation : 
The code iterates over each filepath in the list_of_files . 
filepath = Path(filepath) : Converts the string path to a Path object for easier manipulation. 
filedir, filename = os.path.split(filepath) : Splits the filepath into the directory ( filedir ) and the file name ( filename ). 
if filedir != "": : Checks if filedir is not an empty string, which means the file is located in a directory structure. 
os.makedirs(filedir, exist_ok=True) : Creates the directory (and any intermediate directories) if it doesn't exist. The exist_ok=True parameter prevents raising an error if the directory already exists. 
logging.info(f"Creating directory: {filedir} for the file: {filename}") : Logs a message indicating that the directory is being created. 
if not os.path.exists(filepath) or os.path.getsize(filepath) == 0 : with open (filepath, "w" ) as f: pass logging.info( f"Creating empty file: {filepath} " ) else : logging.info( f" {filename} already exists" ) 6. File Creation : 
if not os.path.exists(filepath) or os.path.getsize(filepath) == 0: : Checks if the file does not exist or if its size is zero (i.e., it's empty). 
with open(filepath, "w") as f: pass : Creates an empty file if the above condition is true. The pass statement is used as a placeholder because we only need to create the file without writing any content to it. 
logging.info(f"Creating empty file: {filepath}") : Logs a message indicating that an empty file is being created. 
else: logging.info(f"{filename} already exists") : If the file already exists and is not empty, logs a message indicating that the file already exists.

Project setup 
Lets Set the project up by filling contents of requrements.txt

e . : This line allows for the installation of your package in editable mode, meaning any changes you make to the package will immediately reflect in the environment without needing a reinstall. 
Next, let’s create setup.py . 
setup.py 
import setuptools with open ( "README.md" , "r" , encoding= "utf-8" ) as f: long_description = f.read() __version__ = "0.0.0" REPO_NAME = "Toxic-Comments-Detection" AUTHOR_USER_NAME = "Harshithvarma007" SRC_REPO = "END_TO_END_MODEL" AUTHOR_EMAIL = "harshith007varma007@gmail.com" setuptools.setup( name=SRC_REPO, version=__version__, author=AUTHOR_USER_NAME, author_email=AUTHOR_EMAIL, description= "A small python package for ml app" , long_description=long_description, long_description_content= "text/markdown" , url= f"https://github.com/ {AUTHOR_USER_NAME} / {REPO_NAME} " , project_urls={ "Bug Tracker" : f"https://github.com/ {AUTHOR_USER_NAME} / {REPO_NAME} /issues" , }, package_dir={ "" : "src" }, packages=setuptools.find_packages(where= "src" ) ) Explanation of setup.py in detail(Skip if you already know): 
Importing setuptools : This library is used to facilitate the packaging of Python projects. 
2. Reading the README.md : 
with open ( "README.md" , "r" , encoding= "utf-8" ) as f: long_description = f.read() This reads the content of README.md for the long description of your package 
3. Defining Package Metadata : 
__version__ = "0.0.0" REPO_NAME = "Toxic-Comments-Detection" AUTHOR_USER_NAME = "Harshithvarma007" SRC_REPO = "END_TO_END_MODEL" AUTHOR_EMAIL = "harshith007varma007@gmail.com" 4. Calling setuptools.setup : 
setuptools.setup( name=SRC_REPO, version=__version__, author=AUTHOR_USER_NAME, author_email=AUTHOR_EMAIL, description= "A small python package for ml app" , long_description=long_description, long_description_content= "text/markdown" , url= f"https://github.com/ {AUTHOR_USER_NAME} / {REPO_NAME} " , project_urls={ "Bug Tracker" : f"https://github.com/ {AUTHOR_USER_NAME} / {REPO_NAME} /issues" , }, package_dir={ "" : "src" }, packages=setuptools.find_packages(where= "src" ) ) name : The name of the package. 
version : The version of the package. 
author : The author’s username. 
author_email : The author’s email. 
description : A short description of the package. 
long_description : A detailed description of the package (content from README.md ). 
long_description_content : The format of the long description. 
url : The URL of the project repository. 
project_urls : Additional URLs related to the project (e.g., bug tracker). 
package_dir : The root directory of the package. 
packages : Automatically finds all packages in the specified directory. 
The setup.py file is a crucial part of packaging a Python project. It provides metadata about the project and instructions on how to install and distribute it 
Now run 
pip install -r requirements.txt 
Custom Logging Creation

import os import sys import logging logging_str = "[%(asctime)s: %(levelname)s: %(module)s: %(message)s]" log_dir = "logs" log_filepath = os . path .join(log_dir, "running_logs.log" ) os .makedirs(log_dir, exist_ok=True) logging.basicConfig( level= logging.INFO, format = logging_str, handlers=[ logging.FileHandler(log_filepath), logging.StreamHandler(sys. stdout ) ] ) logger = logging.getLogger( "Toxic_logger" ) Usage

import os from box.exceptions import BoxValueError import yaml from Toxic_comment_detection import logger import json import joblib from ensure import ensure_annotations from box import ConfigBox from pathlib import Path from typing import Any @ensure_annotations def read_yaml(path_to_yaml: Path) - > ConfigBox: """reads yaml file and returns Args: path_to_yaml (str): path like input Raises: ValueError: if yaml file is empty e: empty file Returns: ConfigBox: ConfigBox type """ try: with open (path_to_yaml) as yaml_file: content = yaml.safe_load(yaml_file) logger.info(f"yaml file: {path_to_yaml} loaded successfully") return ConfigBox(content) except BoxValueError: raise ValueError("yaml file is empty") except Exception as e: raise e @ensure_annotations def create_directories(path_to_directories: list, verbose = True ): """create list of directories Args: path_to_directories (list): list of path of directories ignore_log (bool, optional): ignore if multiple dirs is to be created. Defaults to False. """ for path in path_to_directories: os.makedirs(path, exist_ok = True ) if verbose: logger.info(f"created directory at: {path}") @ensure_annotations def save_json(path: Path, data: dict): """save json data Args: path (Path): path to json file data (dict): data to be saved in json file """ with open (path, "w") as f: json.dump(data, f, indent = 4 ) logger.info(f"json file saved at: {path}") @ensure_annotations def load_json(path: Path) - > ConfigBox: """load json files data Args: path (Path): path to json file Returns: ConfigBox: data as class attributes instead of dict """ with open (path) as f: content = json.load(f) logger.info(f"json file loaded succesfully from: {path}") return ConfigBox(content) @ensure_annotations def save_bin(data: Any , path: Path): """save binary file Args: data (Any): data to be saved as binary path (Path): path to binary file """ joblib.dump( value = data, filename = path) logger.info(f"binary file saved at: {path}") @ensure_annotations def load_bin(path: Path) - > Any : """load binary data Args: path (Path): path to binary file Returns: Any: object stored in the file """ data = joblib.load(path) logger.info(f"binary file loaded from: {path}") return data @ensure_annotations def get_size(path: Path) - > str: """get size in KB Args: path (Path): path of the file Returns: str: size in KB """ size_in_kb = round(os.path.getsize(path) / 1024 ) return f"~ {size_in_kb} KB" Functions : 
read_yaml : Reads a YAML file and returns its contents wrapped in a ConfigBox object. 
create_directories : Creates directories specified in a list of paths, with an option to log the creation. 
save_json : Saves Python data structures as JSON into a specified file path. 
load_json : Loads JSON data from a specified file path into a ConfigBox object. 
save_bin : Saves binary data into a specified file path using joblib . 
load_bin : Loads binary data from a specified file path using joblib . 
get_size : Calculates and returns the size of a file in kilobytes (KB). 
These utility functions provide general-purpose functionality that can be utilized across various end-to-end machine learning projects. They handle operations such as file handling (JSON, binary), directory creation, YAML file reading, and file size retrieval, ensuring efficient and organized project management.

With the rise of LLM models like GPT-4, it has become crucial to develop robust detection mechanisms to ensure the integrity and reliability of text-based communication. 
🔍 Need for Detection of LLM Generated Text 
The need for detecting LLM-generated text arises from several factors: 
Misinformation Control : 🚫 LLMs can spread false information rapidly. Detection helps in identifying and mitigating the impact of misinformation. 
Plagiarism Prevention : 📝 Identifying LLM-generated content assists in preventing academic and content plagiarism, maintaining integrity in research and publications. 
Ethical Considerations : ⚖️ Understanding the origin of text content is crucial for maintaining ethical standards, especially in sensitive areas like news reporting and legal documentation.

🏗️ Let’s Build a TF-IDF Vectorizer for Vectorization : 
🤓 NERD Alert: What is TF-IDF Vectorizer? Why is Vectorization needed? 
Do you have to interrupt me always like this?… Anyways, here is why: 
TF-IDF Vectorizer is a tool used in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval to convert text data into numerical features that can be used for machine learning algorithms. TF-IDF stands for “Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency.” Here’s a brief explanation: 
Term Frequency (TF) : This measures how frequently a term (word) appears in a document. It helps to capture the importance of a word within a specific document. 
Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) : This measures how important a term is within the entire dataset of documents. It helps to reduce the weight of commonly occurring words (e.g., “the,” “is”) that are less informative. 
The product of TF and IDF gives us the TF-IDF score for each word in a document, indicating the word’s significance in that document relative to the entire dataset. TF-IDF Vectorizer converts the text data into numerical vectors based on these scores. 
Vectorization : The process of converting text data into numerical vectors is called vectorization. It is essential for machine learning algorithms because they can only work with numerical data. By transforming text into numerical vectors, we enable the algorithms to process and analyze the text data effectively. 
Now that the nerd is dealt with, let’s move on: 
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer # Initialize the TF-IDF Vectorizer tfidf_vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(max_features= 5000 ) # You can adjust max_features as needed # Tokenize and create TF-IDF vectors for the 'text' column of the combined dataset tfidf_vectors = tfidf_vectorizer.fit_transform(combined_data[ 'text' ]) # Convert TF-IDF vectors to a DataFrame for easy analysis tfidf_df = pd.DataFrame(tfidf_vectors.toarray(), columns=tfidf_vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()) # Display the TF-IDF DataFrame print (tfidf_df.head()) 🎉 Building and Training a Text Classification Model 🎉

You have to realize that models are quite “dumb” 🤓, so we need to label the classes before giving them the data, or else they will throw a fit. That’s why we use a Label Encoder. 
# Encode target labels (0 and 1) using LabelEncoder label_encoder = LabelEncoder() y_train_encoded = label_encoder.fit_transform(y_train) y_test_encoded = label_encoder.transform(y_test) Now the data is ready, and the vectorizer is ready. The only thing left is to build the model. So let’s build a simple neural network for text classification. 
🏗️ Building the Model 
Don’t be fooled by the word “Simple” here 😏. You will soon see how effective this model is. 
# Build a simple neural network model model = Sequential([ Dense( 128 , activation= 'relu' , input_shape=(X_train.shape[ 1 ],)), Dropout( 0.3 ), Dense( 64 , activation= 'relu' ), Dropout( 0.3 ), Dense( 1 , activation= 'sigmoid' ) ]) # Compile the model model. compile (optimizer=Adam(learning_rate= 0.001 ), loss= 'binary_crossentropy' , metrics=[ 'accuracy' ]) 🏋️‍♂️ Training the Model 
Now that the model is built, let’s train it.

Didn’t I tell you? It achieved 99.44% accuracy! It’s amazing! 🌟 
📊 Evaluating the Model 
Let’s further evaluate it. 
# Evaluate the model on the test set test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test_encoded) print ( f'Test Accuracy: {test_accuracy: .4 f} ' ) # Predict probabilities for the test set y_pred_prob = model.predict(X_test) # Convert probabilities to binary predictions (0 or 1) y_pred = (y_pred_prob > 0.5 ).astype( int ) # Calculate and print classification report print ( "Classification Report:" ) print (classification_report(y_test_encoded, y_pred)) # Calculate ROC-AUC score roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test_encoded, y_pred_prob) print ( f"ROC-AUC Score: {roc_auc: .4 f} " ) # Calculate classification report report = classification_report(y_test_encoded, y_pred, output_dict= True ) report_df = pd.DataFrame(report).transpose() # Plotting the classification report as a heatmap plt.figure(figsize=( 8 , 6 )) sns.heatmap(report_df.iloc[:- 1 , :].astype( float ), annot= True , cmap= 'coolwarm' , fmt= '.2f' ) plt.title( 'Classification Report' ) plt.xlabel( 'Metrics' ) plt.ylabel( 'Classes' ) plt.show() # Calculate the confusion matrix conf_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_test_encoded, y_pred) # Plotting the confusion matrix as a heatmap plt.figure(figsize=( 8 , 6 )) sns.heatmap(conf_matrix, annot= True , fmt= 'd' , cmap= 'Blues' ) plt.title( 'Confusion Matrix' ) plt.xlabel( 'Predicted Labels' ) plt.ylabel( 'True Labels' ) plt.show() The model is doing amazing! 🎉 It is able to classify almost perfectly.

import os from box.exceptions import BoxValueError import yaml from LLM_text_detection import logger import json import joblib from ensure import ensure_annotations from box import ConfigBox from pathlib import Path from typing import Any @ensure_annotations def read_yaml ( path_to_yaml: Path ) -> ConfigBox: """reads yaml file and returns Args: path_to_yaml (str): path like input Raises: ValueError: if yaml file is empty e: empty file Returns: ConfigBox: ConfigBox type """ try : with open (path_to_yaml) as yaml_file: content = yaml.safe_load(yaml_file) logger.info( f"yaml file: {path_to_yaml} loaded successfully" ) return ConfigBox(content) except BoxValueError: raise ValueError( "yaml file is empty" ) except Exception as e: raise e @ensure_annotations def create_directories ( path_to_directories: list , verbose= True ): """create list of directories Args: path_to_directories (list): list of path of directories ignore_log (bool, optional): ignore if multiple dirs is to be created. Defaults to False. """ for path in path_to_directories: os.makedirs(path, exist_ok= True ) if verbose: logger.info( f"created directory at: {path} " ) @ensure_annotations def save_json ( path: Path, data: dict ): """save json data Args: path (Path): path to json file data (dict): data to be saved in json file """ with open (path, "w" ) as f: json.dump(data, f, indent= 4 ) logger.info( f"json file saved at: {path} " ) @ensure_annotations def load_json ( path: Path ) -> ConfigBox: """load json files data Args: path (Path): path to json file Returns: ConfigBox: data as class attributes instead of dict """ with open (path) as f: content = json.load(f) logger.info( f"json file loaded succesfully from: {path} " ) return ConfigBox(content) @ensure_annotations def save_bin ( data: Any , path: Path ): """save binary file Args: data (Any): data to be saved as binary path (Path): path to binary file """ joblib.dump(value=data, filename=path) logger.info( f"binary file saved at: {path} " ) @ensure_annotations def load_bin ( path: Path ) -> Any : """load binary data Args: path (Path): path to binary file Returns: Any: object stored in the file """ data = joblib.load(path) logger.info( f"binary file loaded from: {path} " ) return data @ensure_annotations def get_size ( path: Path ) -> str : """get size in KB Args: path (Path): path of the file Returns: str: size in KB """ size_in_kb = round (os.path.getsize(path)/ 1024 ) return f"~ {size_in_kb} KB" Functions : 
read_yaml : Reads a YAML file and returns its contents wrapped in a ConfigBox object. 
create_directories : Creates directories specified in a list of paths, with an option to log the creation. 
save_json : Saves Python data structures as JSON into a specified file path. 
load_json : Loads JSON data from a specified file path into a ConfigBox object. 
save_bin : Saves binary data into a specified file path using joblib . 
load_bin : Loads binary data from a specified file path using joblib . 
get_size : Calculates and returns the size of a file in kilobytes (KB). 
These utility functions provide general-purpose functionality that can be utilized across various end-to-end machine learning projects. They handle operations such as file handling (JSON, binary), directory creation, YAML file reading, and file size retrieval, ensuring efficient and organized project management.

Part III: Continuous Multi-Stage ML Pipeline Development 🚀 
Building a Continuous Multi-Stage ML Pipeline is an exciting ,exhausting and crucial part of any machine learning project. It allows for automation, scalability, and reproducibility, which are essential for maintaining and iterating on machine learning models efficiently. 
🤓 NERD Alert:why is Continuous Multi-Stage ML Pipeline Development needed? 
Continuous Multi-Stage ML Pipeline Development is crucial for several reasons: 
⚙️ Automation and Efficiency: Automates the entire machine learning workflow, from data ingestion to model deployment, reducing manual intervention and saving time. This automation allows data scientists and engineers to focus more on experimentation and model improvement rather than repetitive tasks. 
🌐 Scalability: As models and datasets grow in complexity and size, a well-designed pipeline can handle large volumes of data efficiently. It ensures scalability by enabling easy integration of new data sources and model updates without significant rework. 
🔍 Reproducibility: Ensures that experiments can be replicated consistently, allowing for validation of results and comparisons between different model versions or parameter settings, which is crucial for scientific research and business applications. 
🔄 Flexibility with Dataset Changes: Machine learning projects often encounter changes in datasets. A flexible pipeline design, with modular components for data handling and preprocessing, allows easy adaptation to these changes without rewriting the entire workflow. 
📝 Configuration Management: By using configuration files (e.g., YAML files) for storing dataset paths, model parameters, and other settings, pipelines become adaptable. This separation of configurations from code enables quick adjustments and ensures that changes can be managed systematically. 
🐞 Debugging and Monitoring: Custom logging and error handling within the pipeline provide detailed insights into each stage’s execution. This facilitates debugging by identifying issues promptly and tracking the flow of data and operations through the pipeline. 
🔧 Modularity and Reusability: Organizing the pipeline into modular stages (e.g., data preprocessing, model training, evaluation) enhances reusability. Each stage can be encapsulated as a function or class method, promoting code reuse across different projects or iterations of the same project. 
The Five Stages of an ML Pipeline: Data Ingestion: Acquiring raw data from various sources such as databases, files, or APIs, preparing it for further processing. 
Data Validation: Ensuring data quality and consistency by checking for completeness, correctness, and conformity to expected formats and ranges. 
Data Transformation: Preprocessing data for model readiness, including normalization, feature engineering, and handling missing values. 
Model Training: Using preprocessed data to train machine learning models, optimizing parameters to fit the data and achieve desired outcomes. 
Model Validation: Evaluating model performance using validation techniques such as cross-validation or holdout sets, ensuring the model generalizes well to unseen data. 
Best Practices: During the development of this pipeline, it’s best to start by coding in a notebook environment and later transfer the code to respective files. This approach helps in maintaining clarity and systematic organization throughout the project.

Look at how ‘ham’ is dominating ‘spam’! 😱 Let’s ensure both classes have equal rights. 
NERD: But how do we do that, sir? 
Me: You know, for once you asked the correct question! 👏 
I put my hands in my pocket and bring out the weapon for justice… SMOTE!!! (Screaming like AVADA KEDAVRA!!) 
NERD: Err… but what is this, sir? 
Me: SMOTE stands for Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. It’s a technique used in machine learning, specifically for dealing with imbalanced datasets… 
What is SMOTE? 🤖 
SMOTE addresses class imbalance by generating synthetic samples for the minority class: 
Addressing Class Imbalance: SMOTE tackles the problem where one class (usually minority) has far fewer samples than another class (majority), which can lead to biased models. 
Generating Synthetic Samples: It creates new instances by interpolating between existing minority class samples in the feature space. 
Interpolation Technique: SMOTE selects pairs of similar instances from the minority class and creates synthetic instances along the line segments joining these pairs. 
Maintaining Data Distribution: Synthetic samples maintain the distribution and patterns of the minority class, preventing overfitting and improving model generalization. 
But before we wield SMOTE against this injustice, let’s explore more!

Now, let’s delve into why we use a Count Vectorizer in machine learning. 
📊 Now that we have visualized Data, Let’s Vectorize it! 
NERD: Why Vectorize, sir!? 
Me: If any of you worked in ML long enough, you’d realize models are quite dumb — they only understand numbers! So, a vectorizer is like a translator that converts text into the number language models understand. 🤖 
But for a more sophisticated answer… 
What is a Vectorizer? 🎨 
Text to Numerical Conversion: A vectorizer transforms text data into numerical vectors that machine learning algorithms can process. In NLP, algorithms work with numerical data, so we transform text into a format they comprehend. 
Feature Extraction: Vectorizers extract features from text by converting words or phrases into numerical values. These features capture crucial information like word frequency. 
Dimensionality Reduction: They can reduce text data’s dimensionality by creating matrices where rows are documents and columns are unique words — a sparse representation. 
Why Use Vectorizers? 🚀 
Input Format for Models: ML models need numerical input. Vectorizers convert raw text into a format models can learn from. 
Feature Representation: Captures word importance and relationships, aiding models in learning patterns and making predictions. 
Efficient Data Representation: Provides compact representations, crucial in high-dimensional spaces with many unique words. 
Normalization and Scaling: Although Count Vectorizers don’t normalize or scale inherently, their output can be processed further for better ML algorithm performance. 
Handling Sparse Data: Efficiently manages sparse text data, storing only non-zero values, saving memory and computation. 
In summary, Count Vectorizers are vital for converting text into numerical form, enabling ML models to effectively process and learn from textual data. They capture word frequency, essential for understanding text content and context. 📝 
# Vectorization cv = CountVectorizer() x = df[ 'Message' ] y = df[ 'Category' ].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == 'spam' else 0 ) # Convert labels to binary values x_vectorized = cv.fit_transform(x) now lets use SMOTE! 
# SMOTE oversampling smote = SMOTE(random_state=42) x_resampled, y_resampled = smote.fit_resample(x_vectorized, y) # Plotting class distribution after SMOTE plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6)) sns.countplot(x=y_resampled) plt.title( 'Class Distribution after SMOTE' ) plt.xlabel( 'Category' ) plt.ylabel( 'Count' ) plt.xticks([0, 1], [ 'ham' , 'spam' ]) # Assuming 0 corresponds to 'ham' and 1 corresponds to 'spam' plt.show() NERD: SMOTE is powerful! 🚀 Me (smug): Now that justice is reinforced, let’s get the data ready for the Model. NERD: How do we do that? Me: We will split the data in a standard 80–20 split.

# Build the Deep Learning Model model = Sequential() model. add (Dense( 64 , activation= 'relu' , input_dim=x_train.shape[ 1 ])) model. add (Dropout( 0.7 )) model. add (Dense( 32 , activation= 'relu' )) model. add (Dense( 1 , activation= 'sigmoid' )) # Compile the model model.compile(optimizer= 'adam' , loss= 'binary_crossentropy' , metrics=[ 'accuracy' ]) model.summary() Now that the model is built, let’s train it. 
# Train the model history = model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=32, validation_data=(x_test, y_test), verbose=1) plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) # Plot training & validation accuracy values plt.subplot(1, 2, 1) plt.plot(history.history[ 'accuracy' ]) plt.plot(history.history[ 'val_accuracy' ]) plt.title( 'Model accuracy' ) plt.ylabel( 'Accuracy' ) plt.xlabel( 'Epoch' ) plt.legend([ 'Train' , 'Validation' ], loc= 'upper left' ) # Plot training & validation loss values plt.subplot(1, 2, 2) plt.plot(history.history[ 'loss' ]) plt.plot(history.history[ 'val_loss' ]) plt.title( 'Model loss' ) plt.ylabel( 'Loss' ) plt.xlabel( 'Epoch' ) plt.legend([ 'Train' , 'Validation' ], loc= 'upper left' ) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() Me: Model is doing amazing! 🎉 NERD: But sir, can it be overfitting? Me: You know, for once you make sense. Let’s check with other metrics. 
# Evaluate the model y_pred_prob = model.predict(x_test) y_pred = (y_pred_prob > 0.5 ).astype( int ) accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred) precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred) recall = recall_score(y_test, y_pred) f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred) print ( f'Accuracy: {accuracy: .4 f} ' ) print ( f'Precision: {precision: .4 f} ' ) print ( f'Recall: {recall: .4 f} ' ) print ( f'F1 score: {f1: .4 f} ' ) # Confusion Matrix conf_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred) # Plotting Confusion Matrix plt.figure(figsize=( 8 , 6 )) sns.heatmap(conf_matrix, annot= True , cmap= "coolwarm" , fmt= "d" ) plt.xlabel( 'Predicted label' ) plt.ylabel( 'True label' ) plt.title( 'Confusion Matrix' ) plt.show() Me: Now that the model is evaluated and doing well, let’s save them.

ChatPdf :End to End Gen AI Project 
using Streamlit, Gemini, Langchain and FAISS 
ChatPdf :End to End Gen AI Project 
using Streamlit, Gemini, Langchain and FAISS 
Me: “Are you excited for this, Harry (Assistant)?” 
Harry: “Yes, boss, but no one else seems to share the feeling.” 
Me: “(Sighs) Again, no one in the class?” 
Harry: “Well… there is one guy.” 
Me:“ Don’t tell me… it’s that nerd again!” 
Harry (shrugs): “But he’s the only one who wants to learn from you!” 
Me (veins throbbing on my forehead): “All I think he wants to do is irritate me!” 
Harry: “Boss, if you want, I could AVADA KEDAVRA him!” 
Me: “No, no! That will land you in Azkaban, Harry! We don’t want the wizarding world to know you’re with me. Let’s let him in for now.” 
NERD enters the class. 
Me: “Now, let’s start the class.” 
Project Demo 
Me: “I’m a huge Harry Potter fan!” 
NERD: “Yeah… like that’s real.” 
Me (glancing at my assistant): “Sure, it’s not real at all! Anyway, I uploaded a Harry Potter fanfiction PDF with 1,065 pages and asked it to summarize the battle in the Chamber of Secrets. Here’s the reply:” 
Summary: In the Chamber of Secrets, Harry Potter battles a gigantic basilisk summoned by Tom Riddle. By dodging the basilisk’s lethal gaze and wielding the Sword of Gryffindor, Harry defeats the serpent. However, he is bitten by one of its venomous fangs and becomes fatally wounded. As Harry lies dying, Fawkes the phoenix arrives and heals Harry’s wound with its tears, reviving him. 
In this project, we will create an application that can process multiple PDFs and answer questions based on their content. Not only will we build the app, but we’ll also deploy it ourselves on Streamlit, a user-friendly platform for front-end development. 
We will cover: 
Using Gemini Prop API: Integrate with the Gemini Prop API. 
Managing Secrets in Streamlit: Securely handle sensitive information. 
Familiarity with LangChain: Understand how LangChain fits into the project. 
Before we dive into coding, let’s understand the architecture of this project 
Architecture The entire architecture can be divided into two parts: 
PDF Processing 
Query Handling 
PDF Processing Let’s first convert the PDF document into a text document, as text is more flexible for data transformations. Once we have the text document, we need to divide it into chunks. 
NERD: Why do we have to divide it into chunks? 
Harry (mutters): This guy reminds me of Hermione. 
Me: Imagine we have a 1000-page document and need to retrieve only relevant information. To manage this, we divide the document into chunks and retrieve the relevant chunk. Once we have the text chunks, we need to transform them into a format that computers can understand. We do this by converting the text into embeddings, which can be used for similarity checks. 
Now that we have text embeddings, we store them in a vector store. 
NERD: What is a vector store? 
Harry: Yep! Definitely like Hermione. 
A vector store is a specialized database designed to store and manage vector representations of data, often in the form of embeddings. Here’s a detailed explanation: 
What is a Vector Store? 
Vector Representation: Data (such as text, images, or other types) can be converted into numerical vectors known as embeddings. These vectors are dense, high-dimensional arrays that capture the semantic information of the data. For example, in text processing, a vector might represent the meaning of a word or sentence, allowing comparisons based on their contextual similarity. 
Purpose of Vector Stores: 
Efficient Storage: Vector stores are optimized to store large volumes of vectors in a space-efficient manner and ensure fast access. 
Similarity Search: They enable efficient similarity search and retrieval by quickly finding vectors close to a query vector using distance metrics like Euclidean distance or cosine similarity. 
Key Features: 
Indexing: Vector stores use indexing techniques (e.g., HNSW, Annoy, Faiss) to speed up similarity searches by creating structures that allow for fast nearest-neighbor queries. 
Scalability: They handle large-scale data efficiently, enabling quick retrieval of similar vectors even with millions of embeddings. 
Common Use Cases: 
Recommendation Systems: Matching users with similar products or content. 
Search Engines: Retrieving documents or images similar to a given query. 
Natural Language Processing: Finding similar sentences or phrases. 
Query Handling 
To handle user queries, we first convert the query into an embedding, as we can only perform similarity checks with embeddings. Once we have the query embedding, we can compare it with other embeddings in the vector database. After finding the most relevant embedding, we use this chunk as context for Gemini-1.0-pro, which will generate a response based on this context for the user’s query. 
Me: Now, let’s bring our architecture to life and start coding, one function at a time! 
PDF to Text Conversion 
The get_pdf_text function is responsible for extracting all the text from a PDF document. It works by initializing an empty string, reading the PDF file, and appending the text from each page into this string. Finally, it returns the combined text. 
def get_pdf_text ( pdf_path ): """Extracts text from a PDF document.""" text = "" pdf_reader = PdfReader(pdf_path) for page in pdf_reader.pages: text += page.extract_text() return text 
Text Chunking 
The get_text_chunks function splits the extracted text into manageable chunks. It uses the RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter to divide the text into chunks of up to 10,000 characters, with a 1,000-character overlap between chunks. The function then returns the list of these text chunks. 
def get_text_chunks ( text ): """Splits the extracted text into manageable chunks.""" text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size= 10000 , chunk_overlap= 1000 ) chunks = text_splitter.split_text(text) return chunks 
Creating a Vector Store 
The create_vector_store function creates an in-memory vector store from text chunks. Here’s a quick overview: 
Initialize Embeddings: It uses GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings with a specified model and API key to generate embeddings for the text chunks. 
Create Vector Store: It then uses FAISS.from_texts to build a vector store from the text chunks and their embeddings. 
Return Vector Store: Finally, it returns the created vector store. 
In summary, this function converts text chunks into embeddings and stores them in a vector database for efficient retrieval. 
def create_vector_store ( text_chunks ): """Creates an in-memory vector store from text chunks.""" embeddings = GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings( model= "models/embedding-001" , google_api_key=os.getenv( "GEMINI_API_KEY" ) ) vector_store = FAISS.from_texts(text_chunks, embeddings) return vector_store 
Generating Responses 
The generate_response function creates a detailed and structured response to a question based on the provided context. Here’s a brief explanation: 
Create Prompt: It formats a prompt template using the provided context and question. 
Initialize Model: It creates an instance of genai.GenerativeModel with the model name 'gemini-1.0-pro'. 
Start Chat Session: It begins a chat session with the model. 
Send Prompt: The formatted prompt is sent to the model, which then retrieves a response. 
Return Response: Finally, it returns the response text generated by the model. 
In essence, this function uses a generative AI model to answer a question using the given context, ensuring that the response is detailed and well-structured. 
def generate_response ( context, question ): """Generates a response to a question based on the provided context.""" prompt_template = """ Answer the question as detailed as possible from the provided context. Make sure to provide all the details. If the answer is not in the provided context, just say, "The answer is not in the provided context." Do not provide the wrong answer. and make the answer more visually attractive, structured and precise. Context:\n{context}\n Question:\n{question}\n Answer: """ prompt = prompt_template. format (context=context, question=question) model = genai.GenerativeModel( 'gemini-1.0-pro' ) chat_session = model.start_chat( history=[] ) response = chat_session.send_message(prompt) return response.text 
Handling User Input 
The user_input function handles user queries by generating a response based on a vector store. Here’s a quick breakdown: 
Similarity Search: It performs a search in the vector store to find documents relevant to the user’s question. If it fails, an error is logged, and an error message is returned. 
Extract Context: It combines the text from the retrieved documents into a single context string. 
Generate Response: The generate_response function is then used to produce an answer based on the context and the user’s question. If this fails, an error is logged, and an error message is returned. 
Return Response: Finally, the function returns the generated response. 
In summary, this function searches for relevant documents, extracts context, and generates a response while handling potential errors. 
def user_input ( user_question, vector_store ): """Handles user input and generates a response based on the in-memory vector store.""" try : # Perform similarity search docs = vector_store.similarity_search(user_question) except Exception as e: st.error( f"Failed to perform similarity search: {e} " ) return "Error: Unable to perform the similarity search." # Extracting text from the retrieved documents context = "\n" .join([doc.page_content for doc in docs]) try : # Generate response using the custom function response = generate_response(context, user_question) except Exception as e: st.error( f"Failed to generate response: {e} " ) return "Error: Unable to generate a response." return response

import streamlit as st from PyPDF2 import PdfReader from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_google_genai import GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings import google.generativeai as genai from langchain.vectorstores import FAISS import os import tempfile # Load environment variables from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() # Configure Google Gemini API key from environment variables genai.configure(api_key=os.getenv( "GEMINI_API_KEY" )) # Retrieve login credentials from Streamlit secrets VALID_USERNAME = st.secrets[ "USER_NAME" ] VALID_PASSWORD = st.secrets[ "PASSWORD" ] def get_pdf_text ( pdf_path ): """Extracts text from a PDF document.""" text = "" pdf_reader = PdfReader(pdf_path) for page in pdf_reader.pages: text += page.extract_text() return text def get_text_chunks ( text ): """Splits the extracted text into manageable chunks.""" text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size= 10000 , chunk_overlap= 1000 ) chunks = text_splitter.split_text(text) return chunks def create_vector_store ( text_chunks ): """Creates an in-memory vector store from text chunks.""" embeddings = GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings( model= "models/embedding-001" , google_api_key=os.getenv( "GEMINI_API_KEY" ) ) vector_store = FAISS.from_texts(text_chunks, embeddings) return vector_store def generate_response ( context, question ): """Generates a response to a question based on the provided context.""" prompt_template = """ Answer the question as detailed as possible from the provided context. Make sure to provide all the details. If the answer is not in the provided context, just say, "The answer is not in the provided context." Do not provide the wrong answer. and make the answer more visually attractive, structured and precise. Context:\n{context}\n Question:\n{question}\n Answer: """ prompt = prompt_template. format (context=context, question=question) # Initialize the model with the correct name model = genai.GenerativeModel( 'gemini-1.0-pro' ) # Start a chat session and send the message chat_session = model.start_chat( history=[] ) response = chat_session.send_message(prompt) return response.text def user_input ( user_question, vector_store ): """Handles user input and generates a response based on the in-memory vector store.""" try : # Perform similarity search docs = vector_store.similarity_search(user_question) except Exception as e: st.error( f"Failed to perform similarity search: {e} " ) return "Error: Unable to perform the similarity search." # Extracting text from the retrieved documents context = "\n" .join([doc.page_content for doc in docs]) try : # Generate response using the custom function response = generate_response(context, user_question) except Exception as e: st.error( f"Failed to generate response: {e} " ) return "Error: Unable to generate a response." return response def main (): """Main function to run the Streamlit app.""" st.set_page_config(page_title= "Chat PDF" , layout= "wide" ) # Single Column Layout st.header( "Chat PDF" ) if 'logged_in' not in st.session_state: st.session_state.logged_in = False if not st.session_state.logged_in: st.subheader( "Login" ) username = st.text_input( "Username" ) password = st.text_input( "Password" , type = "password" ) if st.button( "Login" ): if username == VALID_USERNAME and password == VALID_PASSWORD: st.session_state.logged_in = True st.session_state.image_index = 0 # Initialize image index st.success( "Login successful!" ) else : st.error( "Invalid username or password" ) return # Exit early to not show the main app while not logged in # PDF Upload Section pdf_file = st.file_uploader( "Upload PDF" , type = "pdf" ) if pdf_file: # Extract text from the PDF and create an in-memory vector store pdf_text = get_pdf_text(pdf_file) text_chunks = get_text_chunks(pdf_text) vector_store = create_vector_store(text_chunks) st.session_state.vector_store = vector_store # Store in session state # Query Section user_question = st.text_input( "Ask a Question" ) if user_question: if 'vector_store' in st.session_state: vector_store = st.session_state.vector_store response = user_input(user_question, vector_store) st.write( "## Reply:" ) st.write(response) else : st.write( "Please upload a PDF to begin." ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main()

title: Polymath
text:
Polymath 
Master of all trades 
Polymath 
Master of all trades 
Click here to read (if your are not a member) 
Do you ever feel like you’re meant for more? Like you have the potential to be great at not just one thing, but many? If so, you’re not alone. The world has long revered the specialist — those who dedicate their entire lives to mastering a single field. But what if you could be more? What if you could master multiple skills, unlock your full potential, and truly be built differently? Like Batman? Just imagine saying: 
I am Batman. Okay, maybe not literally — but embracing the mindset of mastering multiple skills? Now that’s something real. 
The Rise of the Polymath 
A polymath isn’t just someone who dabbles in different areas. A true polymath achieves mastery across multiple disciplines, driven by relentless curiosity and an insatiable thirst for knowledge. Think of the greats — Leonardo da Vinci, Marie Curie, Benjamin Franklin. These were not just specialists; they were innovators, creators, and visionaries who defied limits. 
But society has conditioned us to think otherwise. From a young age, we are asked, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” — as if choosing one thing defines our entire existence. While specialization has its merits, it often creates tunnel vision, blinding us to the interconnected nature of knowledge. Polymaths, on the other hand, see the bigger picture. They innovate by drawing from multiple disciplines, solving problems in ways that others never consider. 
Breaking Free from Mediocrity 
Being a polymath isn’t about being a nerd or overwhelming yourself with too much knowledge. It’s about choosing curiosity over complacency . 
There is no nobility in mediocrity. The world is filled with people who do the bare minimum to get by. But the ones who stand out, the ones who change the game, are those who never stop learning, who push themselves beyond their comfort zones, and who refuse to be put in a box. 
You were never meant to be just one thing. You were meant to explore, experiment, and evolve. You were meant to be great. 
How to Master Multiple Skills 
Mastery is not reserved for the gifted. It is earned through intentional effort, smart strategies, and a mindset of continuous growth. Here’s how you can start mastering anything in life: 
1. Adopt the Beginner’s Mindset Too often, people give up before they even begin because they fear looking foolish. But every expert was once a beginner. The key is to embrace the learning process, ask questions, and remain open to new ideas. 
2. Learn by Doing The best way to master something is not by endlessly reading about it but by actually doing it. Whether it’s programming, painting, or public speaking — jump in, make mistakes, and refine your skills along the way. 
3. Break It Down into Micro-Skills Every complex skill is made up of smaller, more manageable parts. Instead of trying to master an entire field at once, focus on one sub-skill at a time. For example, if you want to be an entrepreneur, start by mastering problem-solving, communication, and financial literacy separately. 
4. Leverage Cross-Disciplinary Learning One of the most powerful advantages of being a polymath is that you can apply knowledge from one field to another. A designer who understands psychology will create better user experiences. A scientist who studies philosophy will ask better questions. Look for connections between seemingly unrelated skills. 
5. Stay Relentlessly Curious Curiosity is the fuel of mastery. Never stop asking why? and how? Read books outside your main field, talk to experts from different industries, and always remain a student of life. 
6. Surround Yourself with Great Minds You become like the people you spend the most time with. Surround yourself with individuals who challenge you, inspire you, and push you to be better. Learn from them, collaborate, and build a network of thinkers and doers. 
7. Teach What You Learn One of the best ways to solidify your understanding is to teach others. When you explain a concept, you’re forced to break it down into its simplest form, deepening your mastery in the process. 
Why Now is the Best Time to Be a Polymath 
The world is changing faster than ever before. We have access to unlimited knowledge at our fingertips. Online courses, free resources, and global communities make learning easier than at any point in history. There has never been a better time to embrace polymathy. 
So, stop limiting yourself. Stop waiting for permission to explore your interests. Stop believing that you can only be one thing in life. You were designed for more. 
Be relentless. Be curious. Be a polymath. 
The world needs more people like you. 
Yours Truly, 
N Sai Harshith Varma

Click here read if you are not a Medium member 
Ever tried solving a dataset problem at 2 AM with your third cup of coffee in hand, only to realize the real problem was you ? 
Yeah. Same. 
Hi. I’m Harshith. And this isn’t your usual “I built a dashboard, now I’m a data ninja” story. 
This is a story about why I decided to pour my soul — and about 17 mugs of overly strong coffee — into building a full-blown Data + AI/ML project around something that actually matters: student depression. 
🟡 Why: The Part Where I Cried First and Coded Later 
We always start with the Golden Circle: Why → How → What 
So, let’s begin with the “Why”. 
I’ve seen it. You’ve seen it. Heck, you’ve probably felt it. 
That crushing weight of assignments, rejections, fear of failure, not to mention what the hell am I doing with my life moments. As students, we’re often expected to “keep it together,” slap a smile on, and power through it all like caffeine-fueled productivity bots. 
But behind those Instagram stories and neat bullet journals, there’s often a ton of unspoken emotional chaos. 
I built this project because I’ve been there. Because friends of mine have been there. Because some didn’t make it out. 
This project isn’t about grades or building a resume. It’s about trying to use what I’ve learned — data science, machine learning, and empathy — to say: 
“We see you. We hear you. And we’re doing something about it.” 
🛠️ How: Crying into a Dataset (and Making a Dashboard Too) 
I found a dataset on Kaggle that felt too real to ignore. 
It had details like: 
Age 
CGPA 
Academic pressure 
Sleep patterns (or the lack thereof, lol) 
Dietary habits 
Suicidal thoughts 
Family history of mental illness 
Each row? One student. One story. 
What I Did: 
Built a Tableau Dashboard — To visualize depression trends, patterns, and what the data is trying to scream at us. 
Trained an AI/ML Model — To predict which students might be at risk, using features like CGPA, sleep hours, study pressure, etc. 
The goal? Early intervention. Real insights. Real impact. 
🔵 What: The Dashboard, the Model, and Me 
Let’s get nerdy. But also kind. 
This dashboard isn’t just charts and filters. It’s a lens into student mental health , broken into digestible (and beautiful) sections: 
🔹 Overview: The Mental Health Snapshot 
Depression % among students 
Age/gender-wise breakdown 
KPIs (Key Pain Indicators… wait no, wrong abbreviation) 
🔹 Academic Pressure Cooker 
Depression vs. CGPA (surprise: even toppers cry) 
Study satisfaction vs. sadness (yes, it matters) 
Pressure barometer visuals 
🔹 Lifestyle & Sleep: The Midnight Scroll Saga 
Sleep duration vs. depression (spoiler: sleep helps) 
Work/study hour graphs 
What students eat and how it affects their minds 
🔹 Psychosocial Chaos 
Financial stress levels 
Family mental health history 
Suicidal thoughts stat (aka the section that made me stop and breathe) 
And of course, the ML model — a classifier that says: 
“Hey, based on these factors, this student might need help. Let’s not ignore it.” 
💬 Real Talk 
This project taught me more than just data visualization and logistic regression. 
It taught me that behind every datapoint is a person. 
That sometimes, just asking “Are you okay?” matters more than an 85% accuracy score. 
That coding for social good feels better than any Kaggle badge (but hey, those are nice too). 
☕ One More Sip Before We Go 
So here’s to the students crying quietly in library corners. 
To the ones who smile but are screaming inside. 
To the friends who stayed. And to the ones we lost too soon. 
This project is for you. 
And to whoever’s reading this — if you’re struggling, know that it’s okay to not be okay. But it’s not okay to stay silent. 
There’s help. There’s hope. And yes, there’s coffee. Always coffee. 
Stay tuned for the next post, where I actually show you how to build this dashboard like a pro (and maybe with fewer emotional breakdowns). 
With compassion and caffeine, N Sai Harshith Varma

I Analyzed 141,000 Data Jobs — Here’s What the World’s Best Data Professionals Really Earn 
The Real Story Behind Data Professionals’ Salaries in 2025 
I Analyzed 141,000 Data Jobs — Here’s What the World’s Best Data Professionals Really Earn 
The Real Story Behind Data Professionals’ Salaries in 2025 (if you don’t have membership! you can read it here ) 
It started with a simple curiosity. 
What do data professionals really earn these days?” 
That question quickly turned into a rabbit hole. A sprawling JSON file. More than 141,000 job records. Titles you’d expect like “Data Scientist” and “ML Engineer,” and others you might not — “Applied AI Lead”, “Research Team Manager,” or “Analytics Engineering Director.” Salaries from every corner of the world. A spreadsheet so wide it could buckle your browser. 
But the deeper I went, the more I realized something: this wasn’t just about money. It was about people. Careers. Decisions. Dreams. 
So I decided to do something different. 
I built an end-to-end data project that didn’t just crunch numbers but told a story — the story of a data professional’s journey, from raw data to real-world decisions. 
Act 1: The Foundations (Data Engineering) 
Like all good stories, mine began at the bottom. 
The data came in messy. Currency codes all over the place. Salary scales that made no sense (is that 1,200 monthly in ZAR or annually in USD?). Titles were inconsistent, and missing values lurked like landmines. 
Here, the Data Engineer plays the unsung hero. No glory, just grit. GRIT! 
They build the pipelines, clean the garbage, standardize formats, and make sure everything flows. I wrangled the JSON into structured tables, normalized currencies, dropped outliers, and made sure our foundation was solid. Because if the data is bad, everything built on top of it will crumble. 
BUT… this Dataset was too clean! I was low-key hoping for a mess so I could flex some data-cleaning muscles. Now I’m just sitting here with my unused pandas skills 😩🐼 
Act 2: Making Sense of the Chaos (Data Analysis) 
Enter the Data Analyst . 
Their job?(or my job in this case) To ask smart questions, get meaningful answers and build stunning visualizations. 
I poured my heart, soul, and probably a few brain cells into this Dashboard — so the least you can do is favorite it and throw in a nomination. Don’t make me beg… but I will. 😉 
The Global Landscape: A Six-Figure Standard The first look at the data confirms what many suspect: a career in data is lucrative. The average salary sits at a healthy $157,497 . However, the median salary, at $146,148 , tells a more nuanced story. This gap reveals a key truth about the industry: while most professionals are well-compensated, a cohort of high-earners pulls the average up, creating a “long tail” of exceptional salaries reaching well beyond $400,000. 
For the vast majority, the financial sweet spot lies between $100,000 and $180,000 . Geographically, this gold rush is centered in North America , which stands out as the world’s highest-paying region, with Western Europe following as a strong second. 
Climbing the Career Ladder: From Entry Level to Expert Experience, unsurprisingly, is the primary driver of compensation. The journey from an entry-level position to a senior role comes with a distinct and significant financial reward. But what’s more interesting is how the salary landscape changes with seniority. For entry-level professionals, salaries are relatively tightly clustered. As you advance, however, the range of possible earnings explodes. 
This increased variance at the senior and experienced levels means that while a baseline of high pay is expected, there is immense potential for top performers to far exceed their peers. These high-earning outliers, visible at every stage of the career ladder, prove that exceptional skill in a high-demand niche pays a premium. 
The Two Paths to the Top: Specialization and Leadership So, how does one become a top earner? Our analysis reveals two clear paths. 
The first is specialization . While foundational roles like “Data Scientist” and “Data Engineer” are the most common in the industry, they are not the highest paying. The top of the salary pyramid is occupied by highly specialized roles. In today’s market, AI and Machine Learning are king. Titles like “Research Team Lead,” “Analytics Engineering Manager,” “Applied AI/ML Lead,” and “Head of Machine Learning” command the highest salaries, often exceeding $350,000. 
The second path is leadership . Moving into management roles like “Director of Data” or taking on “Lead” responsibilities is a proven strategy for reaching the upper echelons of compensation. The takeaway is clear: to maximize earnings, one must either go deep into a technical specialty or go broad into management. 
The Company and the Commute: Where You Work Matters Beyond your role, the company you work for plays a crucial part. As expected, large-sized companies offer the highest average salaries, leveraging their resources to attract top talent. Geographically, the market is dominated by US-based companies hiring US-based employees , though a healthy pattern of international hiring shows that talent is a global commodity. 
But perhaps the most profound shift has been in how we work. The data reveals a tectonic change that has redefined the professional landscape. 
The Post-2021 Boom: A Remote Revolution After a brief dip in 2021, data professional salaries have skyrocketed, surging from just under $100,000 to over $156,000 by 2025. This explosive growth signals a massive, industry-wide demand for data skills in the post-pandemic economy. 
Running parallel to this salary boom has been the unstoppable rise of remote work. What began as a necessity has become the new standard, with fully remote and hybrid roles steadily replacing traditional in-office positions. But this isn’t just a story about flexibility; it’s a story about compensation. Our analysis reveals a striking final insight: fully remote (WFH) roles are now the highest-paying work arrangement , averaging over $159,000. 
The modern data career is no longer tied to a specific office or even a specific country. It is a story of continuous learning, strategic specialization, and embracing the freedom of a global, remote-first talent market. 
What We Discovered 
At the end of this journey, here’s what we learned: 
Careers in data are lucrative, but unequal . Averages hide the extremes. 
Experience pays — but specialization or leadership is the real unlock. 
Remote is the new headquarters . The best-paying jobs aren’t tied to geography anymore. 
Everyone plays a role . From engineers to analysts, scientists to managers — the data journey is a team sport. 
Why This Project Matters 
Because data isn’t just zeros and ones. It’s about people — people trying to build better futures. Whether you’re: 
A student choosing between career paths 
A recruiter figuring out competitive salaries 
A company designing your compensation structure 
Or a data nerd (like me) just curious about where you stand… 
This project helps you see the full picture. 
And more importantly, it shows you how to build that picture, piece by piece. 
What’s Next 
In Part 2 of our story, I’ll take the engineered features and dive deeper into building predictive models . We’ll compare algorithms, analyze performance, and explore what it really takes to forecast the future of your career. 
Because in the world of data, the best way to understand tomorrow… is to build it today. 
Yours Truly, N Sai Harshith Varma
