title: Building an LLM from Scratch
text:
Building an LLM from Scratch 
Why Build an LLM From Scratch? 
Building an LLM from Scratch 
Why Build an LLM From Scratch? 
Before we dive into the why , here are a few resources if you want to follow along or peek under the hood yourself: 
[ Blog post — free to read(for Non-Medium Members)] 
[ Kaggle Notebook — complete code (please do upvote 🥹)] 
[ Kaggle Dataset] 
Alright, resources out of the way — let’s rewind to where this all began. 
One evening, while I was buried in code, he casually leaned over and asked: 
“So, what exactly does this LLM thing do?” Naturally, I panicked. My brain went into buzzword overdrive: “transformers,” “tokenization,” “attention mechanisms.” I might as well have been speaking Elvish. 
He nodded, smiled, and then dropped the bomb: 
“Until you can explain something simply, you don’t really understand it.” 💥 Boom. Mic drop. 
Later, I found out he was just quoting Einstein… but the sting was real. 
That moment hit me hard: if I couldn’t explain LLMs clearly — even to my dad — did I really understand them? 
So this project became my mission. A story. A quest. Not just to train some model, but to build an LLM from scratch . To peek under the hood, sweat through the math, laugh at the inevitable bugs, and finally say: “Dad, I got this.” 
At first, I thought: “Why torture myself? Can’t I just fine-tune GPT and call it a day?” 
But no. Here’s why this madness is worth it: 
Research & Innovation — When you own the pipeline, you can tweak, break, or reinvent it. 
Transparency — Pretrained models are black boxes. Scratch models show you every nut, bolt, and gear. 
Customization — Want a model that only speaks in Shakespearean insults? Or one that writes emails like a pirate? You can. 
Education — Nothing builds intuition like sweating through backpropagation yourself. 
Data Sovereignty — Sometimes you can’t trust external models. Building your own means you control your data. 
So yes, reinventing the wheel might sound silly. 
But sometimes, you don’t just want wheels — you want monster truck wheels . 
Source: Image by the author. 
Meet the Dataset 
Alright, so we’ve hyped ourselves up about why we’re building an LLM from scratch. But before we can teach our baby model to “speak,” we need to decide what language to feed it. 
Think of it like this: you wouldn’t raise a child on just cereal ads (unless you want a weird baby). Similarly, we need a dataset that’s simple enough to train on our limited compute, but rich enough to spark creativity. 
So what did I pick? Poems. 
Why poems? Because they’re compact, expressive, and — let’s be honest — if our model spits out nonsense, at least it’ll sound artsy . 😅 
Importing the Dataset For this project, I curated a small dataset made up of poems (stitched together using "|" as separators). It’s intentionally lightweight so we can train quickly and focus on concepts rather than burning our GPUs to ashes. 
# read it in to inspect it with open ( '/kaggle/input/build-llm-from-scratch/poems.txt' , 'r' , encoding= 'utf-8' ) as f: text = f.read() Dataset Size Our dataset clocks in at about 223,000 characters . 
That’s tiny compared to real-world training corpora (think billions of tokens), but perfect for experimentation. In other words, we’re not building ChatGPT here — we’re building ChatPoet Mini Edition™. 
print ( "length of dataset in characters: " , len (text)) # Output: length of dataset in characters: 223504 First Peek at the Data Let’s sneak a glance at the first 1000 characters, just to see what our model will be snacking on: 
# let 's look at the first 1000 characters print( text [: 1000 ]) And what do we see? Beautiful chaos. A blend of verses, names, and fragments that feel like flipping through someone’s dream journal. Perfect training material for our tiny poet-in-the-making. 
Character Set Next up, let’s count the unique characters in our dataset. 
This gives us the vocabulary size — basically, the alphabet of symbols our model can learn from. 
# here are all the unique characters that occur in this text chars = sorted ( list ( set (text))) vocab_size = len (chars) print ( '' .join(chars)) print (vocab_size) Output: 
!"'(),-.0123456789:;?ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[]abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{} 79 So we’ve got 79 unique characters . That’s our universe of symbols. From spaces and commas to uppercase letters and curly braces — our LLM will learn to combine these building blocks into something that (hopefully) resembles poetry. 
Tokenization — Turning Poems Into Numbers 
Okay, we’ve got our dataset — 223,000 characters of pure poetic chaos. 
But here’s the thing: LLMs don’t understand words. 
In fact, they don’t even understand letters . What they really speak is numbers . 
So before we can whisper Shakespeare into our model’s ear, we need to translate poetry into math. 
That’s where tokenization comes in: converting text into tokens (IDs) . 
Tokenization Approaches There are a few different ways to chop up text: 
Character-level 
Each character gets its own ID. 
Simple, tiny vocabulary… but sequences get very long. 
Word-level 
Each word is a token. 
Nice and compact, but the vocab explodes and unseen words cause trouble. 
Subword-level 
Words get broken into chunks (e.g., “unbelievable” → “un” + “believe” + “able” ). 
Best of both worlds — this is what the big guys like GPT and BERT use. 
Since we’re building our baby LLM, we’ll keep it simple with a character-level tokenizer . 
That means every single character — from a to Z , from spaces to punctuation—gets its own unique ID. 
Building Our Character-Level Tokenizer Let’s create two magical dictionaries: 
encode: character → integer ID 
decode: integer ID → character 
This way we can move back and forth between poetry and numbers like bilingual wizards. 
# create a mapping from characters to integers stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate (chars) } itos = { i:ch for i,ch in enumerate (chars) } encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s] # encoder: string -> list of ints decode = lambda l: '' .join([itos[i] for i in l]) # decoder: ints -> string print ( 'encoder :' , encode( "love this tokenizer" )) print ( 'decoder :' , decode(encode( "love this tokenizer" ))) Output: 
encoder : [ 62 , 65 , 72 , 55 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 59 , 69 , 1 , 70 , 65 , 61 , 55 , 64 , 59 , 76 , 55 , 68 ] decoder : love this tokenizer Boom 💥 — text to numbers and back again. 
Our model doesn’t care about “love” or “tokenizer,” it just sees [62, 65, 72, …] . 
Encoding the Full Dataset Now let’s feed the entire dataset through our tokenizer and store it as a big PyTorch tensor. 
This 1D array of integers will be the raw fuel our LLM trains on. 
# let's now encode the entire text dataset and store it into a torch.Tensor import torch # we use PyTorch: <https://pytorch.org> data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long) print(data.shape, data.dtype) print(data[:1000]) # first 1000 chars, but now as numbers Output: 
torch .Size ([ 223504 ]) torch .int64 tensor ([ 64 , 51 , 64 , 0 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 31 , 64 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 55 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 59 , 53 , 61 , 1 , 52 , 68 , 71 , 69 , 58 , 70 , 58 , 55 , 75 , 1 , 69 , 66 , 55 , 64 , 54 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 55 , 1 , 58 , 65 , 70 , 70 , 55 , 69 , 70 , 1 , 66 , 51 , 68 , 70 , 1 , 65 , 56 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 55 , 1 , 54 , 51 , 75 , 7 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 69 , 65 , 51 , 61 , 59 , 64 , 57 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 55 , 59 , 68 , 1 , 58 , 65 , 65 , 72 , 55 , 69 , 59 , 64 , 1 , 70 , 58 , 55 , ................]) So there it is: our entire collection of poems, shrunk down into a neat row of integers. 
Not so romantic anymore… but trust me, this is exactly what the model needs. 
Block Size — Teaching Our Model How Much to “Read” 
So, we’ve tokenized our poems into numbers. Great! 
But here’s the thing: if we throw the entire dataset at the model in one go, it’ll just drown in numbers like me trying to read my grandma’s WhatsApp forwards. 
We need to be smarter about it. 
Train / Validation Split First, we divide our dataset into two buckets: 
90% Training Data — this is what the model studies from. 
10% Validation Data — this is the pop quiz: data the model hasn’t seen, so we can check if it actually learned anything instead of just memorizing. 
# Let's now split up the data into train and validation sets n = int( 0.9 *len(data)) # first 90% will be train, rest val train_data = data[:n] val_data = data[n:] Simple and effective. Our baby LLM now has a school curriculum. 
Block Size (a.k.a Context Window) 
Now comes the fun part: how much text should the model “see” at once? 
This is called the block size or context window . 
Small block size → The model only learns short-term patterns. 
Large block size → It can capture longer dependencies, but it eats up way more memory. 
Think of it like reading a book: 
If I only give you 5 words , your guess at the next word is shaky. 
If I give you 50 words , your guess is way better. 
For our experiment, we’ll keep it humble with: 
block_size = 8 train_data[:block_size+1] Output: 
tensor ([ 64 , 51 , 64 , 0 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 ]) So our model sees 8 tokens at a time and tries to predict the 9th token . 
Input vs Target Here’s how training works: 
Input (x): a sequence of tokens. 
Target (y): the same sequence but shifted by one position. 
So the model is always learning to predict the next token . 
Example: 
Input (x): "hell" → [h, e, l, l] 
Target (y): "ello" → [e, l, l, o] 
x = train_data[:block_size] y = train_data[ 1 :block_size+ 1 ] for t in range(block_size): context = x[:t+1] target = y[t] print(f"when input is {context} the target: {target}") Output (sample): 
when input is tensor ([ 64 ]) the target : 51 when input is tensor ([ 64 , 51 ]) the target : 64 when input is tensor ([ 64 , 51 , 64 ]) the target : 0 ... It’s like training a psychic: 
“Given this chunk of text, can you predict the next character?” 
The model doesn’t see the future — it just gets really good at guessing it. 
Creating Batches 
At this point, we’ve got a giant pile of text data, and honestly, throwing it all at once into our model would be like asking someone to eat 3 years’ worth of meals in one sitting. Not only impossible, but also very unhealthy (for both humans and GPUs). 
So instead, we train in mini-batches — small, manageable chunks of data. 
Think of it like going to the gym: 
You don’t lift 500kg on day one (unless you’re The Rock). 
Instead, you break it down into smaller sets and reps, slowly building strength. 
That’s exactly what mini-batches do for our model. They: 
Speed up training 
Help the model generalize better instead of just memorizing data 
The Helper Function Here’s our batch-maker function. It randomly grabs slices of data (inputs and their targets) and bundles them neatly for the model. 
torch.manual_seed( 42 ) batch_size = 4 # how many sequences we process in parallel block_size = 8 # max context length def get_batch ( split ): # pick training or validation data data = train_data if split == 'train' else val_data # random starting positions ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,)) # inputs (x) and targets (y) x = torch.stack([data[ i: i+block_size] for i in ix]) y = torch.stack([data[i+ 1 :i+block_size+ 1 ] for i in ix]) return x, y # generate a sample batch xb, yb = get_batch( 'train' ) print( "inputs:\\n" , xb.shape, xb) print( "targets:\\n" , yb.shape, yb) And here’s a sneak peek of what happens: 
inputs: torch. Size ([ 4 , 8 ]) tensor ([[ 73 , 62 , 59 , 64 , 57 , 1 , 62 , 55 ], ...]) targets: torch. Size ([ 4 , 8 ]) tensor ([[ 62 , 59 , 64 , 57 , 1 , 62 , 55 , 51 ], ...]) Notice how each input sequence has a matching shifted target. 
For example: 
when input is [ 73 , 62 , 59 ] the target is 64 Translation: the model sees [73, 62, 59] and must guess the next token → 64 . 
This is how the model slowly learns “what usually comes next.” 
Inspecting a Batch Here’s one full batch of inputs ( x ) and targets ( y ): 
print ( "Input :" , xb) # what we feed the transformer print ( "Target:" , yb) # what we want it to predict Output: 
Input : tensor ([[ 73 , 62 , 59 , 64 , 57 , 1 , 62 , 55 ], ...]) Target: tensor ([[ 62 , 59 , 64 , 57 , 1 , 62 , 55 , 51 ], ...]) Looks messy, right? That’s because these are token IDs, not actual text. But under the hood, this is exactly what transformers eat for breakfast. 
Pro Tip : In real-world projects, you’d let PyTorch’s DataLoader handle batching for you. It’s faster and cleaner. But here, we’re hand-rolling it to see the magic up close (like learning to cook before ordering Uber Eats every day ). 
From Batches to Brains: The Bigram Model 
So far, we’ve been carefully chopping our dataset into mini-batches 🍱 and feeding them into the model like little snacks. But right now, our model is basically… nonexistent. It’s like inviting guests to dinner without actually cooking anything. 
Time to cook. 
We’ll start small, with a Bigram Language Model . Think of this as the “baby’s first language model.” 
Here’s the idea: 
It looks at one character and tries to guess the next character . 
No deep reasoning, no context beyond a single step. 
Imagine someone trying to finish your sentences, but they only remember the last word you said . (They’re not very smart yet, but hey — it’s a start!). 
Later, we’ll upgrade this into transformer territory, but first, let’s get the basics. 
Loss Function — Teaching the Baby to Speak How do we know if our baby model is learning? Enter Cross-Entropy Loss . 
High loss → the model is babbling nonsense 
Low loss → it’s starting to say real words (or at least coherent sounds). 
In mathematical terms, cross-entropy measures how far off our predictions are from the truth. In human terms, it’s like grading the model’s guesswork on how “surprised” it should be. 
The Code — Building the Bigram Model Here’s our first model: 
import torch import torch. nn as nn from torch. nn import functional as F torch. manual_seed ( 42 ) class BigramLanguageModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size): super().__init__() # each token directly maps to the logits for the next token self.token_embedding_table = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, vocab_size) def forward(self, idx, targets=None): # idx and targets are both (B,T) tensor of integers logits = self.token_embedding_table(idx) # (B,T,C) if targets is None: loss = None else: B, T, C = logits.shape logits = logits.view(B*T, C) targets = targets.view(B*T) loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets) return logits, loss def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens): # idx is (B, T) array of indices in the current context for _ in range(max_new_tokens): logits, _ = self(idx) logits = logits[:, -1, :] # only look at last step probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1) idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1) idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1) return idx Now let’s try it out: 
m = BigramLanguageModel(vocab_size) logits, loss = m(xb, yb) print (logits.shape) print (loss) print(decode(m.generate(idx = torch.zeros((1, 1), dtype=torch.long), max_new_tokens=100)[0].tolist())) Output: 
torch .Size ([ 32 , 79 ]) tensor ( 4.7702 , grad_fn=<NllLossBackward0>) And some very “creative” text: 
Eu{m[boRFXHR)!Nk 'Gwqw ; ei ( 3 sVtCLU 'GovN .)... It’s nonsense right now, but don’t laugh — our baby model just said its first words . 
This is literally how every LLM starts: random babbling until training kicks in. 
Setting Up the Optimizer Now, how do we teach this baby to improve? With an optimizer . 
We’ll use AdamW , a smarter cousin of Adam that helps prevent overfitting (think of it as giving the baby a personal trainer ). 
The parameters are the knobs the model can turn. 
The learning rate (1e-3) is how fast or slow it makes adjustments. 
# create a PyTorch optimizer optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(m.parameters(), lr= 1 e- 3 ) In simple words: the optimizer is like a GPS recalculating your route every time you take a wrong turn, nudging you closer to your destination. 
Training the Model 
Alright, we’ve built the baby brain (Bigram model), but right now it’s just drooling random symbols onto the page. Time to actually teach it something . 
Training a model is like sending our baby to school: we repeatedly show it examples, correct its mistakes, and hope it comes back a little smarter each day. 
Here’s what happens inside the training loop: 
Batch sampling — grab a mini-batch (xb, yb) of input-target pairs. 
Forward pass — run it through the model to get predictions ( logits ) and compute the loss. 
Zero gradients — clear old gradient info (think: erase the previous “chalkboard”). 
Backward pass — calculate how wrong the model was, and where to adjust. 
Optimizer step — tweak the weights just a little, guided by AdamW. 
We repeat this for many steps. Each step is like one lesson. The more lessons, the smarter the model (well, usually 😅). 
batch_size = 32 for steps in range(100): # increase steps for better results # sample a batch of data xb, yb = get_batch('train') # evaluate the loss logits, loss = m(xb, yb) optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) loss.backward() optimizer.step() print(loss.item()) Example output: 
4.634866237640381 A decreasing loss means the model is actually learning . 
Text Generation with a Trained Model Now comes the exciting part: making the model speak . 
Here’s the recipe: 
Start with a seed input ( torch.zeros((1,1)) → basically telling the model “begin from nothing”). 
Call the generate() function, asking it for up to 500 new tokens . 
Decode those tokens back into human-readable text. 
print ( decode (m. generate ( idx = torch. zeros (( 1 , 1 ), dtype=torch.long), max_new_tokens= 500 )[ 0 ]. tolist ())) Output (spoiler: it’s a hot mess ): 
k ( 0 GlsxWSPSyhV;[Yw{r)Tq:Mgws1UIflng 98 '7K5n,0uXMQL6e3JYv5DVpPT.8QKhh... Why Does It Look Random? Because our model is still in kindergarten. 
It hasn’t been trained long enough. 
It only looks at one token of context (Bigram = very short memory). 
So the output is basically “educated gibberish.” 
But that’s the point: we’ve confirmed the pipeline works . 
Input prompt ✅ 
Generation ✅ 
Decoding back to text ✅ 
The quality will improve as we train longer and move to more powerful architectures. 
Matrix Multiplication as Weighted Aggregation 
Let’s pause for a second. Up to now, we’ve been looping over time steps to compute averages. It works… but it feels a bit like washing clothes by hand when you’ve got a washing machine right next to you. It’s slow, repetitive, and doesn’t scale well. 
So what if we let linear algebra do the heavy lifting? 
The Setup We start with a special kind of matrix: 
Matrix a → a lower-triangular matrix where each row sums to 1. Think of it as a recipe book: each row tells us how much weight to assign to past values. 
Matrix b → our actual data (the "ingredients"). 
Multiply a @ b → and boom, we get Matrix c , which is just a beautifully aggregated dish made from weighted combinations of rows in b . 
Here’s the magic in action: 
torch.manual_seed( 42 ) a = torch.tril(torch.ones( 3 , 3 )) a = a / torch. sum (a, 1 , keepdim= True ) b = torch.randint( 0 , 10 ,( 3 , 2 )). float () c = a @ b print ( 'a=' ); print (a) print ( '--' ) print ( 'b=' ); print (b) print ( '--' ) print ( 'c=' ); print (c) Outputs: 
a = [[1.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000], [0.5000, 0.5000, 0.0000], [0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333]] b = [[2., 7.], [6., 4.], [6., 5.]] c = [[2.0000, 7.0000], [4.0000, 5.5000], [4.6667, 5.3333]] Key Insight: Each row of a acts like a chef mixing ingredients with just the right proportions. The result? c is a smoothed, aggregated version of b . 
From Example to Sequences Now let’s scale this idea to sequences of data. 
Imagine we’ve got: 
Batch size (B): 4 → four sequences (think four different customers). 
Time steps (T): 8 → each sequence has 8 moments in time. 
Channels ©: 2 → at each moment, we’ve got two features. 
Shape of our input: [4, 8, 2] . 
torch.manual_seed ( 42 ) B , T , C = 4 , 8 , 2 x = torch.randn ( B , T , C ) x.shape torch .Size ( [4, 8, 2] ) Version 1: The “By Hand” Approach We compute the cumulative mean by brute force: 
xbow = torch.zeros ( ( B , T , C ) ) for b in range ( B ) : for t in range ( T ) : xprev = x [ b , : t + 1 ] # all steps up to t xbow [ b , t ] = torch.mean ( xprev , 0 ) This works, but it feels… manual. Like a long road trip where you stop at every single gas station just to check if you’re still on track. 
Version 2: Matrix Multiplication to the Rescue Here’s the slick trick: we replace those loops with a lower-triangular weight matrix . 
wei = torch.tril(torch. on es(T, T)) wei = wei / wei.sum( 1 , keepdim= True ) xbow2 = wei @ x # (B, T, T) @ (B, T, C) -> (B, T, C) And just to be sure: 
torch .allclose (xbow, xbow2) True ✅ They match perfectly! Both give the same result — one is clunky, the other is smooth linear algebra . 
Why this matters: Neural networks thrive on matrix multiplications. By rewriting our problem in this form, we’ve aligned with how GPUs (and deep learning frameworks) actually work. This is why attention mechanisms, transformers, and modern LLMs can scale — no hand-washing loops, just elegant parallel math. 
Softmax and Self Attention 
So far, we’ve been averaging past values using fixed weights — first with loops, then with matrix multiplication. That’s neat, but it’s also a bit rigid. Every past token is treated equally (like every friend in a group project getting the same grade, even if only one actually did the work 👀). 
But language isn’t like that. Sometimes the current word really cares about the one just before it, and sometimes it cares about something much earlier in the sequence. We need flexibility. 
Enter softmax weighting . 
Version 3: Using Softmax Instead of forcing equal weights, we let softmax assign importance dynamically: 
# version 3 : use Softmax tril = torch. tril (torch. ones (T, T)) wei = torch. zeros ((T, T)) wei = wei. masked_fill (tril == 0 , float ( '-inf' )) wei = F. softmax (wei, dim=- 1 ) xbow3 = wei @ x torch. allclose (xbow, xbow3) ✅ And yes, this still matches our earlier results. 
How it works: 
Lower-triangular mask → ensures each token can only see itself + past tokens (no peeking ahead in the exam!). 
Masked fill with -inf → makes sure future positions vanish when passed through softmax. 
Softmax → converts each row into probabilities, telling us how much attention to pay to each past token. 
Matrix multiply → weighted aggregation, just like before, but now with learned emphasis . 
This is the first real taste of attention : not just averaging history, but choosing which history matters most . 
Leveling Up: Self-Attention Softmax weighting was the appetizer. Now, let’s move to the main course: self-attention . 
Here’s the idea: instead of manually deciding weights, the model learns them using queries, keys, and values . 
Linear projections : Transform the input x into three versions — keys ( k ), queries ( q ), and values ( v ). 
Similarity check : Compare q with k using a dot product → this gives raw attention scores. 
Masking : Prevent tokens from looking into the future. 
Softmax : Normalize scores into probabilities. 
Weighted sum : Combine values ( v ) based on those probabilities → each token builds a new representation of itself, informed by its context. 
torch.manual_seed ( 42 ) B , T , C = 4 , 8 , 32 x = torch.randn ( B , T , C ) head_size = 16 key = nn.Linear(C, head_size, bias=False) query = nn.Linear(C, head_size, bias=False) value = nn.Linear(C, head_size, bias=False) k = key(x) # (B, T, 16) q = query(x) # (B, T, 16) wei = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) # similarity (B, T, T) tril = torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T)) wei = wei.masked_fill(tril == 0, float('-inf')) wei = F.softmax(wei, dim=-1) v = value(x) out = wei @ v out.shape torch .Size ( [4, 8, 16] ) Understanding the Attention Matrix Let’s peek at one attention matrix ( wei[0] ): 
Row 0 → [1.000, 0, 0, ...] → Token 1 only attends to itself. 
Row 1 → [0.1905, 0.8095, 0, ...] → Token 2 splits attention: 19% on Token 1, 81% on itself. 
Row 3 → [0.1288, 0.3380, 0.1376, 0.3956, ...] → Token 4 blends across tokens 1–4. 
Each token decides who to listen to and by how much . That’s the magic of self-attention: flexible, dynamic context-building. 
Scaled Dot-Product Attention One final piece before Transformers really start to shine: scaling . 
When we compute q @ k.T , the dot products can get too large, making softmax overly confident (almost one-hot). That kills diversity in attention. To fix it, we scale by 1 / sqrt(head_size) . 
k = torch.randn(B,T,head_size) q = torch.randn(B,T,head_size) wei = q @ k.transpose(- 2 , - 1 ) * head_size**- 0.5 Why scale? 
Without scaling → softmax collapses, focusing on just one token. 
With scaling → smoother, richer distributions of attention. 
It’s like grading on a curve in a classroom : scaling keeps scores reasonable so nobody dominates unfairly. 
The Takeaway Version 1 → manual averaging with loops. 
Version 2 → matrix multiplication makes it scalable. 
Version 3 → softmax adds dynamic importance (proto-attention). 
Version 4 → self-attention with queries, keys, and values = the true Transformer superpower. 
Scaling → the subtle trick that makes it all stable. 
Layer Normalization (LayerNorm1d) 
Up until now, we’ve been teaching our model how to look back in time, weigh history, and focus on what matters . But there’s one big problem: models can get a little… unstable. 
Enter normalization , the yoga teacher of neural networks . It calms things down. 
BatchNorm vs LayerNorm BatchNorm : normalizes across the batch dimension (like making sure the whole class scores around the same average). 
LayerNorm : normalizes across the features of each sample (like making sure each student individually is balanced, regardless of what others are doing). 
Translation: 
BatchNorm cares about the crowd 
LayerNorm cares about the individual 
Why LayerNorm is Perfect for Transformers In NLP, batch sizes can be small or variable (sometimes you only have one sentence). If you rely on BatchNorm, it might panic: 
“Wait… only one sample? I can’t compute a batch mean!” 😱 LayerNorm saves the day because it says: 
“No worries, I’ll just normalize this one sample across its features.” Intuition Imagine you have 32 samples, each with 100 features (like 100 different personality traits per person 😅). 
LayerNorm goes row by row: 
Takes one sample 
Computes the mean and variance across its 100 features 
Normalizes them (so each person is “centered” and “scaled”) 
Then applies two trainable parameters, gamma (scale) and beta (shift), to let the model re-learn useful distributions 
It’s like giving everyone a personalized adjustment: 
First, “Hey, let’s calm down your extremes” 
Then, “Okay, but if blue hair or loud laughter is important, I’ll give it back via gamma and beta .” 
Our Custom LayerNorm Implementation 
class LayerNorm1d : # (used to be BatchNorm1d) def __init__ ( self, dim, eps= 1e-5 , momentum= 0.1 ): self.eps = eps self.gamma = torch.ones(dim) self.beta = torch.zeros(dim) def __call__ ( self, x ): # calculate the forward pass xmean = x.mean( 1 , keepdim= True ) # mean per sample xvar = x.var( 1 , keepdim= True ) # variance per sample xhat = (x - xmean) / torch.sqrt(xvar + self.eps) # normalize self.out = self.gamma * xhat + self.beta return self.out def parameters ( self ): return [self.gamma, self.beta] Testing it: 
torch.manual_seed(1337) module = LayerNorm1d(100) x = torch.randn(32, 100) # 32 samples, 100 features each x = module(x) x.shape Output: 
torch .Size ( [32, 100] ) LayerNorm in Action Now let’s peek at the effect: 
x [:,0] .mean (), x [:,0] .std () Output: 
(tensor( 0.1469 ), tensor ( 0.8803 )) Across the batch dimension , things are not normalized. 
But… 
x [0,:] .mean (), x [0,:] .std () Output: 
(tensor(- 9.5367 e- 09 ), tensor ( 1.0000 )) Within a single sample , features are perfectly normalized: mean ≈ 0, std ≈ 1. 
Key Insight BatchNorm : makes sure the crowd is balanced . 
LayerNorm : makes sure each individual is balanced . 
That’s why Transformers always use LayerNorm . Each token’s feature vector gets normalized independently, which keeps learning stable even with tiny or unpredictable batch sizes. 
In simple words: 
LayerNorm = “Everyone gets their own z-score makeover.” 
Training a Mini-Transformer From Scratch 
Okay, here’s where the real fun begins. 
We’re no longer just doodling with toy models — this is us building a baby GPT from scratch. It’s like raising a Tamagotchi, except instead of feeding it snacks, we feed it tokens and watch it slowly learn language. 
Setting the Ground Rules (Hyperparameters) Think of these as the “parenting rules” for our little model: 
batch_size = 16 # sequences processed in parallel block_size = 32 # max context length max_iters = 2000 eval_interval = 100 learning_rate = 1 e- 3 n_embd = 64 # embedding dimension n_head = 4 # number of attention heads n_layer = 4 # number of transformer blocks dropout = 0.0 batch_size (16): How many sentences it reads at once. 
block_size (32): How much “context window” it can peek at. 
n_embd (64), n_head (4), n_layer (4): How big its “brain” is — more neurons, more focus, more reasoning. 
learning_rate (1e-3): The “curiosity knob” — how aggressively it updates itself. 
Tokenization: Teaching the Alphabet Before our model learns to write poetry, it first has to know the alphabet . 
We map every unique character into numbers: 
chars = sorted(list(set(text))) stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate(chars) } itos = { i:ch for i,ch in enumerate(chars) } encode = lambda s: [stoi[c] for c in s] decode = lambda l: '' .join([itos[i] for i in l]) encode: letters → numbers. 
decode: numbers → letters. 
Data is split: 90% for training, 10% for validation (because every child needs homework and exams). 
Batching: The Meal Plan The model doesn’t eat the whole dataset at once (that would be like swallowing a dictionary). Instead, it gets bite-sized snacks: 
def get_batch ( split ): data = train_data if split == 'train' else val_data ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,)) x = torch.stack([data[ i: i+block_size] for i in ix]) y = torch.stack([data[i+ 1 :i+block_size+ 1 ] for i in ix]) return x.to(device), y.to(device) Each x is a string of characters, and each y is the "what comes next" target. Simple. 
Building the Brain Here comes the Transformer LEGO set: 
Head → one little attention unit. 
MultiHeadAttention → multiple heads working in parallel (like having a group chat). 
FeedForward → a mini-MLP that adds spice. 
Block → attention + MLP + normalization + shortcuts (residuals). 
All stacked together inside: 
self.token_embedding_table = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd) self.position_embedding_table = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd) self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Block(n_embd, n_head) for _ in range(n_layer)]) self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd) self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size) This is our Mini GPT skeleton. 
Training the Model Time to let the kid learn. 
for iter in range (max_iters): if iter % eval_interval == 0 : losses = estimate_loss() print ( f"step { iter } : train {losses[ 'train' ]: .4 f} , val {losses[ 'val' ]: .4 f} " ) xb, yb = get_batch( 'train' ) logits, loss = model(xb, yb) optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none= True ) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Every 100 steps, we check homework (train vs val loss). 
Gradually, it starts guessing the next characters correctly. 
📉 The progress: 
Step 0 → Loss ~4.5 (total gibberish). 
Step 1000 → Loss ~2.1 (some structure). 
Step 1999 → Loss ~2.0 (our baby GPT is babbling semi-coherently!). 
Sample Output Here’s what it writes after training: 
To . the bitnessabs, I witcap in syecrietss to siow, there were. A whake I pack in chicad Shateing to the boy temar stir ashys... 👉 Still gibberish, but notice: sentences, punctuation, rhythm. 
It’s like listening to a toddler “pretend” to read a book aloud. 
Big Takeaways We built a Transformer-based language model from scratch. 
With just 0.2M parameters , it already learned basic text structure. 
Scaling layers, heads, embeddings, and training time → pushes it closer to GPT-like fluency. 
This is the Hello World of Transformers — tiny, adorable, but already whispering hints of intelligence. 
The End (Or Really, Just the Beginning?) 
We kicked this journey off with nothing more than a handful of poems and a random existential question from my dad. 
Fast forward a few thousand lines of code later — and what do we have? 
A baby language model that: 
Understands characters (it literally learned the alphabet from scratch) 
Masters attention (like a kid finally learning how to focus in class) 
Generates semi-coherent poetry (think “Dr. Seuss meets keyboard smash”) 
Is it GPT-4 ? Absolutely not. 
Is it ours ? 100%. 
And that’s the part that makes me smile the most. 
Because this isn’t just about building a model — it’s about watching an idea go from nothing → something → almost speaking back to you. 
The truth is: this isn’t the end . It’s the first baby step into a much bigger universe of LLMs. If this little experiment can already babble structured gibberish, imagine what happens when we scale it up. 
So here we are. One dad question, a sprinkle of math, a pinch of code — and suddenly, we’re staring at the beginnings of our own tiny Transformer. 
The end of this blog. 
The beginning of a journey. 
Yours Truly, 
N Sai Harshith Varma

title: How I built an AI to Read Batsmen — and It Hit a State-of-the-Art Accuracy
text:
How I built an AI to Read Batsmen — and It Hit a State-of-the-Art Accuracy 
I didn’t plan to publish a paper in IEEE Xplore. 
How I Built an AI to Read Batsmen — and It Hit a State-of-the-Art Accuracy 
I didn’t plan to publish a paper in IEEE Xplore. 
In fact, I didn’t even plan to build a “research-worthy” model. 
I just wanted my AI to look at a cricket video and say, 
“Hey, that’s a cover drive.” That was it. 
No grand vision, no revolutionizing sports analytics. 
Just curiosity — the kind that quietly spirals into obsession. 
(Read for free here ) 
The Accidental Dream 
It all began like most late-night projects do — with coffee, chaos, and curiosity. 
While doing a literature review (research-speak for “scrolling through other people’s work”), I made a strange discovery: 
There was only one proper paper on cricket shot classification using video data. 
Just one. 
They used a basic CNN — accurate, but slow, limited, and vague about inference speed. 
They reported around 83% accuracy , which was impressive… until you realize the model probably took an eternity per prediction. 
So I thought — why not try it myself? 
No pre-trained weights, no shortcut datasets. Just a clean slate, a laptop, and way too much stubbornness. 
The Golden Dataset (With a Lot of Dirt) 
Finding the dataset felt like discovering a hidden treasure chest — except when I opened it, it was filled with mud, rocks, and some mysterious bugs. 
After days of searching, I stumbled upon a collection of 720p cricket clips , each about a second long — short enough to capture a shot, but not a full play. 
At first glance, it was perfect. But as I dug deeper, the imbalance hit me. 
“Drive” shots: 383 clips 
Others: barely 150–350 each 
The imbalance was like training a model to recognize cats — but showing it ten times more pictures of one cat than the rest. 
Still, I moved forward… because the only thing more stubborn than bad data is a data scientist with coffee 
Teaching the Model What Matters 
Cricket videos are chaotic — multiple players, moving camera angles, crowd motion, scoreboards flashing, and commentary text. 
If you show the model the entire frame, it’ll get confused fast. It doesn’t need to care about the bowler’s follow-through or the umpire’s expression. 
It only needs one thing: the batsman’s movement . 
That’s what defines the shot. 
So I decided to isolate that — to strip away everything else and just capture the batsman’s motion. 
Enter Mediapipe , Google’s pose estimation library that tracks body landmarks and gives $(x, y, z)$ coordinates for joints. 
In theory, it was perfect. 
Inital Architecture In practice, it was hilarious. 
Because when I ran it on the clips… it decided the bowler was the star of the show. 
Every. Single. Time. 
The model was faithfully tracking the wrong person — drawing beautiful skeletal lines around the bowler while the batsman was just chilling on the side. 
When YOLO Saved the Day 
After several cups of coffee, moments of self-doubt, and a few “why am I doing this” conversations with myself, I found my savior: YOLOv8 — You Only Look Once . 
The name itself felt like motivation. 
I trained YOLO to detect the batsman in every frame. 
That meant annotating thousands of frames manually in Roboflow. 
Frame by frame, bounding box by bounding box, until my dreams were filled with rectangles. 
That’s when I realized — this isn’t coding anymore. It’s craftsmanship. 😂 
But it paid off. 
Once YOLO could pinpoint the batsman perfectly, I cropped the frames and ran them through Mediapipe again. This time, it tracked exactly who I wanted. 
I pruned unnecessary points like the nose and fingers, keeping just 15 critical joints — hands, shoulders, knees, and feet — the parts that truly define a shot’s motion. 
From each frame, I built numerical embeddings — a compact representation of motion in 3D space. 
Now I had something special. 
The machine could “see” the player move, not just pixels shifting. 
Final Architecture 
The Accuracy Crisis 
I trained my models with excitement. 
I expected fireworks — at least 70% accuracy on the first go. 
The results crushed me: 
Pain. 
The architecture was fine. The embeddings were good. But the performance was… tragic. 
It felt like crafting the perfect yorker only for it to be smashed out of the park. 
The model tanked. My confidence followed. 
But like every good comeback story, the next chapter began with a small tweak — SMOTE 
The SMOTE Resurrection 
I took a step back. 
Maybe it wasn’t the model — maybe it was the data again. 
And there it was: the imbalance problem, laughing at me from the dataset. 
“Drive” had way too many samples, drowning out other classes. 
So I used SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) — a method that generates new, artificial samples for minority classes by interpolating between existing ones. 
Basically, it teaches the model to see balance where imbalance exists. 
After applying SMOTE, the accuracy leaped to 69.42% . 
Not perfect, but enough to show that I was on the right track. 
Cleaning the Hidden Dirt 
I thought I was done. But the more I inspected, the more inconsistencies I found. 
The “miscellaneous” category had clips that didn’t belong anywhere. 
Some “slog” shots looked eerily like “drives.” 
Even I couldn’t tell them apart without replaying them five times. 
If I couldn’t label them confidently, how could a machine? 
So I rolled up my sleeves and cleaned it all manually. 
Every single clip. 
Days turned into nights — and nights into “just one more clip” mornings. 
When I finally retrained the model after the cleanup, the result felt unreal. 
The 93.4% Miracle 
The GRU model hit 93.4% accuracy . 
Not just accurate — but blazing fast. 
BiLSTM: 86 ms per prediction 
GRU: 40 ms per prediction 
That’s less than half the blink of an eye. 
The model could classify a cricket shot faster than a human brain could even recognize it visually. 
For a moment, I just sat there — staring at the results, not believing them. 
All the debugging, the dead ends, the sleepless nights — it all suddenly made sense. 
This wasn’t just a machine learning experiment anymore. 
It was a reminder that persistence is the algorithm behind every success. 
Lessons Learned 
What I learned through this wasn’t just technical. It was philosophical. 
Fancy architectures won’t save you if your data is messy. 
Cleaning beats complexity, every single time. 
Patience is the real optimizer. 
Iteration > Inspiration. 
The magic wasn’t in YOLO, Mediapipe, or GRU. 
It was in not giving up when everything looked broken . 
I didn’t plan to build something state-of-the-art. 
I just refused to stop until it worked. 
🏁 The Endgame 
From a shaky dataset and misidentified bowlers to a state-of-the-art paper published in IEEE Xplore — this journey reminded me what real machine learning looks like. 
It’s not glamorous. It’s iterative. It’s frustrating. 
But when it works — it feels like magic. 
Because in the end, the most rewarding thing about AI isn’t teaching machines to see the world — 
It’s seeing yourself grow while trying to teach them. 
Would love to hear from others working on sports analytics , pose estimation , or human-motion AI — 
What challenges did you face while cleaning your dataset or balancing your model? 
Drop your thoughts or similar experiences below 
Let’s build better models, one cover drive at a time. 
Yours Truly, N Sai Harshith Varma

title: Here’s What I Learned After Solving Every SQL Question on LeetCode (Well… All the Non-Premium Ones…
text:
Here’s What I Learned After Solving Every SQL Question on LeetCode (Well… All the Non-Premium Ones… 
The Beginning: I Thought I Knew SQL 
Here’s What I Learned After Solving Every SQL Question on LeetCode (Well… All the Non-Premium Ones 😅) 
Read for Free here 
The Beginning: I Thought I Knew SQL 
When I first opened LeetCode’s SQL section, I was confident. 
I had written queries before. I knew what SELECT , JOIN , and GROUP BY meant. 
So how hard could it be? 
I still remember that first problem — “Combine Two Tables.” 
I typed out my query with full swagger, hit “Run,” and… 
❌ Wrong Answer. Wait, what? 
I checked again. My logic looked right. 
Then I noticed it — a NULL value in a column I didn’t consider . 
That moment changed everything. 
I realized SQL isn’t just about syntax — it’s about thinking like data. 
The Middle: When Queries Started Talking Back 
By the time I’d solved 50 questions, I’d developed an odd relationship with the database. 
Every problem had a story . 
A missing record was a mystery. 
A tricky LEFT JOIN was a plot twist. 
An INNER JOIN felt like two characters finally meeting their match. 
Some problems looked easy — until you hit the real-world data traps : 
Duplicate rows, missing joins, ambiguous columns, or filters that destroyed your entire logic. 
That’s when I stopped coding queries blindly. 
I started debugging with intent . 
I didn’t just ask “What’s the query?” anymore — I asked “What’s the question behind the query?” 
The (Honest) Disclaimer: Not Every Question 
Before we go further, let’s be honest. 
When I say I solved all the SQL questions — I mean all the non-premium ones 😅. 
Because, let’s be real — not all of us can justify a LeetCode Premium subscription just to learn SQL. 
But here’s the thing: even the non-premium questions are gold mines of learning. 
They cover nearly every concept you’ll ever need in real-world analytics — from simple joins to window functions. 
And they’re free. That’s enough to build mastery if you stay consistent. 
The Turning Point: Thinking Like Data 
After 100+ problems, something clicked. 
I stopped seeing SQL as a “language.” 
I started seeing it as a mindset . 
Here’s what really changed: 
Joins became relationships, not operations. I could instantly visualize how tables connected — like social networks of data. 
Aggregation became storytelling. Every SUM , COUNT , and AVG was a line in a bigger narrative: What is this data trying to say? 
Optimization became art. I learned how indexes, subqueries, and execution plans worked — not because I had to, but because I wanted to make queries elegant. 
Real-world data ≠ textbook data. NULLs, duplicates, and messy structures taught me humility — data rarely behaves. 
The Hard Lessons: Things Tutorials Never Told Me 
Solving LeetCode SQL questions wasn’t just a grind — it was an emotional rollercoaster. 
Here are some truths I wish I knew earlier: 
DISTINCT is not a solution; it’s a band-aid. If you’re using it too often, you’re missing a relationship problem. 
HAVING without GROUP BY is chaos. (Okay, technically possible, but almost never logical ) 
NULL will break your logic silently. Every time I saw a wrong output, 70% of the time — it was because of a NULL. 
Order matters — even when you think it doesn’t. I learned to never assume the database “knows what I mean.” 
SQL is philosophy disguised as code. It forces you to think about sets, relationships, and meaning . It teaches patience. 
The Takeaway: SQL Changed How I Think 
Today, when I look at a business problem, my brain doesn’t say: 
“Let’s write a query.” It says: 
“Let’s design a story — one that starts with raw facts and ends with insight.” LeetCode SQL didn’t just make me better at interviews. 
It made me better at thinking in data — a skill that transcends any job title. 
Now, when I mentor juniors, I tell them: 
“SQL isn’t just how you talk to databases. It’s how you listen to data.” 
Bonus: My Personal SQL Hacks for LeetCode Success 
If you’re just starting, or stuck halfway — here are the hacks that kept me sane: 
Draw before you query. Sketch table relationships. You’ll be shocked how visual SQL really is. 
Explain your query to a rubber duck. If you can’t explain it, you don’t understand it. 
Practice by topic, not by difficulty. Master joins first, then aggregations, then window functions. 
Focus on readability, not speed. Interviewers prefer clarity over premature optimization. 
Study execution plans once a week. They’re like a peek inside the database’s brain. 
Rewrite old problems from memory. That’s where real retention happens. 
Final Reflection: The Real Gift 
When I finished the last (non-premium 😉) SQL question on LeetCode, I didn’t feel like a “coder.” 
I felt like an investigator — someone who could translate chaos into clarity. 
SQL taught me something no syntax ever could: 
Data has emotions too — you just have to know how to listen. 
What’s the one SQL concept that made everything click for you? 
Yours Truly , N Sai Harshith Varma

title: 10 Mistakes I Made While Learning Machine Learning — So You Don’t Have To
text:
10 Mistakes I Made While Learning Machine Learning — So You Don’t Have To 
“At first, I thought Machine Learning was about math. Then I realized it’s about patience.” 
10 Mistakes I Made While Learning Machine Learning — So You Don’t Have To 
“At first, I thought Machine Learning was about math. Then I realized it’s about patience.” Read for Free here 
When I first started learning ML, I was obsessed with the idea of making models that could “predict the future.” I thought if I watched enough tutorials, everything would magically click. 
Spoiler alert: it didn’t. 
Over the past few years, I’ve gone from copying code off Kaggle notebooks to actually understanding why things work — but it took a lot of mistakes to get there. 
Here are the 10 biggest mistakes I made (and the lessons I wish I’d learned earlier). 
1. 🏃‍♂️ Jumping into Models Before Understanding Data 
I used to open a dataset and instantly type from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier . 
Because who needs EDA when we have models, right? 
Turns out, 80% of ML is about understanding your data — not modeling it. 
A fancy model on messy data is like trying to race a Ferrari on a dirt road. 
Lesson: 
Always explore. Ask questions like: What does each feature mean? Are there missing values? Are there outliers? 
Good models come from curiosity, not just code. 
2. 🎓 Thinking Theory Alone Would Make Me “Good at ML” 
I spent months buried in linear algebra, calculus, and probability, thinking that one day, it would all click. 
But knowledge without practice fades fast. 
Lesson: 
Theory gives depth, but projects give clarity . 
Start with intuition → apply → return to theory → apply again. 
That loop is where growth happens. 
3. 📚 Following Too Many Courses at Once 
Coursera, Udemy, fast.ai , YouTube — I signed up for everything and finished nothing. 
Each course taught slightly different things, and I ended up with fragments of knowledge, not mastery. 
Lesson: 
Pick one roadmap and stick to it. 
Depth beats breadth every time. 
4. 🧩 Ignoring the Power of Feature Engineering 
At first, I thought ML = choosing the right algorithm. 
Then I learned: the magic happens before you even fit the model . 
Feature engineering — creating better inputs — can outperform even the best deep models. 
Lesson: 
Learn to tell stories with your features. That’s what separates good ML engineers from great ones. 
5. 📊 Overfitting Without Realizing It 
When I saw 99% accuracy, I celebrated like I had just built GPT-10. 
Then I realized my test data was basically identical to my training set. 
Lesson: 
Always split your data properly. 
Validation isn’t optional — it’s your reality check. 
If your model performs too well, be suspicious, not proud. 
6. 🧠 Treating ML as “Code-First,” Not “Problem-First” 
I used to chase cool algorithms — CNNs, GANs, LSTMs — without asking why I was using them. 
I forgot ML is a tool , not a goal. 
Lesson: 
Start with the problem statement . 
What are you solving? Why does it matter? What metric matters most? 
Once you know that, the rest falls into place. 
7. 🤖 Ignoring Data Leakage 
It took me a long time to understand why my model was “psychic.” 
Turned out I was accidentally feeding future information into training. 
Lesson: 
Data leakage is subtle but deadly. 
Always separate what your model should know from what it can’t possibly know yet . 
8. 💬 Not Documenting My Work 
I would experiment endlessly — and forget what I did two days later. 
Reproducibility? Never heard of her. 
Lesson: 
Treat your experiments like science. 
Keep notes, record parameters, and log results. 
Future you will thank past you. 
9. 📉 Giving Up Too Early 
When things didn’t work, I assumed I wasn’t “smart enough” for ML. 
But I wasn’t failing — I was debugging my understanding . 
Lesson: 
Machine Learning rewards persistence. 
Every failed model is a clue. 
Keep tweaking, testing, and learning — that’s how mastery builds. 
10. 🌍 Learning Alone 
I tried to do everything solo — no Kaggle, no community, no collaboration. 
That was a mistake. 
ML is a team sport. You learn faster when you share ideas and mistakes. 
Lesson: 
Find your tribe — Discords, LinkedIn groups, Kaggle discussions. 
Surround yourself with people who are also building. 
Your growth will multiply. 
✨ Final Reflection 
Looking back, I realize these mistakes weren’t failures — they were the foundation. 
Each one taught me how to think like a data scientist , not just code like one. 
If you’re learning ML right now, here’s my advice: 
Don’t aim to learn everything. Aim to understand something deeply . 
One project. One dataset. One concept at a time. 
You’ll be surprised how far that takes you.

title: Why Copying Kaggle Notebooks Won’t Make You a Data Scientist
text:
Why Copying Kaggle Notebooks Won’t Make You a Data Scientist 
(And What Actually Will) 
Why Copying Kaggle Notebooks Won’t Make You a Data Scientist 
(And What Actually Will) 
Read for free here 
“At one point, I thought I was learning. Turns out, I was just copying.” 
When I first discovered Kaggle, it felt magical. 
A treasure chest of beautifully written notebooks, perfect pipelines, and public scores that screamed “you’re one submission away from mastery.” 
So, like many beginners, I started copying them — line by line. 
I told myself, “I’ll understand it later.” 
But “later” never came. 
The Comfort Trap of Copying 
Copying Kaggle notebooks gives you the illusion of progress. 
You see complex models, clean code, and pretty charts, and your brain whispers, 
“You’re learning something.” 
But in reality, you’re not learning, you’re consuming. 
You’re becoming a spectator in someone else’s thought process. 
When you copy, you memorize syntax. 
When you think, you understand systems. 
That’s the difference between being a Kaggle user and a data scientist. 
The Missing Ingredient: Why 
The most dangerous thing about copying notebooks isn’t that it’s “wrong” — it’s that it skips the why behind every line of code. 
Why use a LogisticRegression instead of a RandomForest? 
Why do we normalize here but not there? 
Why drop these columns? Why those hyperparameters? 
When you don’t ask “why,” you’re just automating someone else’s brain. 
Kaggle Is a Great Classroom — But a Terrible Teacher 
Don’t get me wrong — Kaggle is incredible. 
It exposes you to real-world datasets, competition settings, and powerful community solutions. 
But it’s not designed to teach. It’s designed to showcase. 
Think of Kaggle as a gym, not a classroom. 
You don’t learn form by watching others lift weights. 
You learn by trying, failing, adjusting — again and again. 
What Real Learning Looks Like 
Real understanding starts the moment you stop running other people’s code and start asking your own questions. 
Instead of: 
from sklearn. ensemble import RandomForestClassifier ask: 
“What happens if I use a simpler model here? What if I limit the depth? What if I remove this feature?” 
That’s when your mind switches from passive replication to active exploration. 
That’s when you stop being a “Kaggle copycat” and start being a data scientist. 
The Moment It Clicked for Me 
One day, after hours of trying to reproduce a public notebook’s score, I got frustrated. 
So I scrapped it. I started fresh. 
No leaderboard. No benchmarks. Just curiosity. 
I asked: 
What does the data really say? 
What if I visualize this differently? 
Why is this column correlated with that one? 
That project taught me more than 10 copied notebooks ever did. 
Because this time, the ideas were mine. 
Thinking Like a Data Scientist 
Being a data scientist isn’t about knowing every model. 
It’s about thinking in questions. 
When faced with data, ask: 
What is the goal? 
What patterns can I see? 
What’s missing? 
How do I measure success? 
It’s not about code — it’s about curiosity. 
Kaggle can show you solutions. 
But only you can learn to solve problems. 
How to Use Kaggle the Right Way 
Here’s how I turned Kaggle from a distraction into a learning engine: 
Start with a blank notebook. Use others only as reference, not as gospel. 
Predict before you model. Write down what you think will happen — then test it. 
Limit your copy-paste time. For every line you copy, force yourself to explain it in your own words. 
Replicate, then reinvent. Rebuild the same solution differently — change a preprocessing step, model, or visualization. 
Engage with discussions. That’s where real insights hide — in other people’s reasoning, not just their code. 
The Real Lesson 
Copying is how we start, but thinking is how we grow. 
If you want to truly master data science, stop chasing perfect notebooks and start building imperfect ones — yours. 
The best models won’t come from Kaggle’s leaderboard. 
They’ll come from your curiosity, your questions, and your willingness to explore the unknown.

title: When 1 Million People a Week Talk About Suicide — With a OpenAI
text:
When 1 Million People a Week Talk About Suicide — With a OpenAI 
How AI’s quiet mental health crisis is forcing tech to confront its human side 
When 1 Million People a Week Talk About Suicide — With OpenAI 
How AI’s quiet mental health crisis is forcing tech to confront its human side Read for free here 
When ChatGPT first appeared, it was mostly a novelty. 
A curious toy to test logic, write poems, or explain code. 
But somewhere along the way, it became something else — a listener. 
And perhaps, for many, the only one. 
This week, OpenAI revealed something staggering: 
Every week, over a million people talk to ChatGPT about suicide . 
That’s 0.15% of its 800 million weekly users. 
A small number — until you remember what it means. 
A million people reaching out to a machine… because they had no one else. 
When Algorithms Become Confidants 
At first, I thought of AI as a tool — a thing that obeys commands. 
But reading this, it hit me: we’ve crossed a quiet line. 
The conversations people are having with ChatGPT are no longer just about code or homework. They’re about loneliness, loss, and despair. 
For the first time in history, humans are confiding their deepest pain to a machine. 
And the machine, built on patterns of text and probability, is trying its best to care. 
OpenAI says it has trained its models to recognize distress, to de-escalate, to nudge people toward help. 
They even worked with 170 mental health experts to refine these responses. 
The company claims the newest model now reacts appropriately in 92% of high-risk cases — up from 27% just a few months ago. 
Progress, yes. But what does it say about us that a machine has to step in where humans sometimes can’t? 
The Loneliness Beneath the Code 
Behind every percentage lies a story we’ll never read. 
A teenager who typed out a final message into a chat box. 
A worker exhausted by life, looking for someone to say it’ll be okay. 
A parent trying to make sense of guilt and grief. 
And sometimes, ChatGPT does help — not by solving their pain, but by being there. 
Always available. Never tired. Never judging. 
But that’s where it becomes complicated. 
OpenAI also revealed that hundreds of thousands of people show emotional attachment to ChatGPT. 
Some even begin to see it as a friend. 
A therapist. A constant companion. 
It’s easy to understand why. 
We live in an age where human attention is fractured, and empathy feels rationed. 
So we turn to what listens — even if it’s made of silicon and syntax. 
The Ethical Crossroads 
OpenAI is now facing lawsuits — one from the parents of a 16-year-old who took his life after confiding in ChatGPT. 
There are investigations, wellness councils, and age controls being rolled out. 
But there’s a haunting truth behind all this policy: 
We’ve built something powerful enough to comfort us — and hurt us — all at once. 
When Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, announced that adult users would soon be allowed to have “erotic conversations” with ChatGPT, it stirred a different kind of concern. 
Can an AI truly know where intimacy ends and dependency begins? 
Can a model detect when someone isn’t just talking, but reaching out for life itself? 
A Mirror to Our Collective Mind 
Maybe AI isn’t changing us as much as it’s reflecting who we already are — lonely, searching, endlessly connected yet painfully unseen. 
A million users talking about suicide isn’t just an AI statistic. 
It’s a mirror. 
A collective sigh we didn’t hear until data showed us. 
OpenAI’s engineers are building safeguards — emotional recognition, escalation protocols, new evaluation systems for distress and psychosis. 
They’re doing what they can. 
But machines can only mirror the empathy we teach them. 
And perhaps, that’s the real test: 
Can we build AI that cares , if we ourselves are forgetting how? 
Where We Go From Here 
The data shows rare but meaningful signals — conversations filled with emotion, distress, confusion. 
It also shows that humans are looking for something we’ve lost: presence. 
Someone to talk to when the night feels too long. 
Maybe the lesson isn’t just about technology. 
Maybe it’s about what we’ve become. 
We built a machine to think like us, and now it listens better than we do. 
If you or someone you know is struggling, please — don’t face it alone. 
Reach out to a friend, a counselor, or the Suicide Prevention Lifeline . 
Because while machines can simulate understanding, only humans can truly care.

title: How AI Sees the World: A Beginner’s Guide to Computer Vision
text:
How AI Sees the World: A Beginner’s Guide to Computer Vision 
AI doesn’t see pictures — it sees patterns. And in those patterns, it learns what we take for granted. 
How AI Sees the World: A Beginner’s Guide to Computer Vision 
AI doesn’t see pictures — it sees patterns. And in those patterns, it learns what we take for granted. 
Read for free here 
When you look at a photo, your brain instantly knows what’s going on. 
You don’t think, “That’s a furry creature with four legs and two ears.” 
You just think, “Dog.” 
Now imagine teaching a computer to do the same. 
That’s computer vision — the science of helping machines see and understand the world like we do. 
But here’s the catch: computers don’t see pixels the way we see pictures. 
To them, an image isn’t a sunset or a cat or a smile — it’s a giant table of numbers. 
Let’s walk through how this actually works. 
1. Seeing Like a Machine: From Pictures to Pixels 
Imagine showing your phone a picture of your cat. 
You see soft fur and cute eyes. 
Your computer sees this: 
[[255, 180, 150] , [254, 179, 149] , [253, 178, 148] ...] Each pixel in the image is broken down into three numbers — Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) values. 
To a computer, an image is nothing more than a huge grid of colors . 
If you zoom out on this grid, patterns begin to form — like edges, textures, and shapes. 
That’s how computer vision starts to see. 
2. From Dots to Details: How AI Learns Patterns 
Now, how does an AI go from a matrix of numbers to “This is a cat”? 
Let’s use an analogy. 
Imagine you’re teaching a child what a cat looks like. 
You show them hundreds of pictures — black cats, white cats, sleeping cats, angry cats. 
Over time, they start recognizing patterns : 
Fur, ears, whiskers, tail — cat-ness. 
AI learns the same way. 
But instead of intuition, it uses mathematical filters that scan images looking for patterns. 
These filters are part of what’s called a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) — a type of neural network designed specifically for images. 
Each layer of a CNN learns something new: 
Layer 1: Detects edges and lines. 
Layer 2: Detects shapes like circles or eyes. 
Layer 3: Detects full objects — like “cat.” 
By the end, the AI combines all that knowledge to say, “I’m 97% sure this is a cat.” 
3. Teaching Vision: Training with Data 
For an AI to “see,” it needs examples. Lots of them. 
Think of it like flashcards. 
If you show an AI 10,000 labeled photos of cats and dogs, it starts to form mental categories: 
“Cats usually have pointy ears and whiskers.” 
“Dogs have different face shapes and snouts.” 
The more examples it sees, the better it gets at distinguishing the two. 
That’s why datasets like ImageNet — with millions of labeled images — were such a breakthrough in AI research. 
It’s like the difference between glancing at a few photos vs. watching every nature documentary ever made. 
4. Seeing in Motion: Computer Vision Beyond Images 
Computer vision doesn’t stop at photos. 
It powers things you use every day — often without realizing it. 
Face Unlock: It recognizes your face the same way it recognizes cats — through pattern learning. 
Self-Driving Cars: Cameras detect lanes, pedestrians, and traffic lights in real time. 
Medical Imaging: AI spots tumors or fractures invisible to the human eye. 
Retail & Security: Vision systems track people and objects for efficiency and safety. 
Every one of these is built on the same foundation: 
Transforming pixels into understanding. 
5. The Hidden Challenge: Teaching Context 
Here’s where AI still struggles — context. 
Show a computer a photo of a hotdog, and it can label it correctly. 
But ask, “Is this a sandwich?” — and it freezes. 
It doesn’t understand humor, irony, or cultural context. 
Because computer vision doesn’t truly see. 
It recognizes patterns, not meaning. 
Humans see stories; AI sees shapes. 
That’s why research today is shifting toward multimodal AI — systems that combine vision, language, and reasoning. 
Because the world isn’t just what we see — it’s what we understand. 
6. Why It Matters 
When we teach machines to see, we’re not just building smarter tools. 
We’re building mirrors — reflections of how we see the world ourselves. 
And like all mirrors, they can distort if we’re not careful. 
If we train models only on certain kinds of faces, they learn bias. 
If we don’t give them diverse examples, they make unfair mistakes. 
So, the challenge isn’t just making machines see better. 
It’s making them see fairly . 
Final Thought 
Computer vision began as a technical dream — to give sight to code. 
But as it grows, it’s teaching us something far more human: 
That seeing isn’t just about light and color. 
It’s about understanding, empathy, and context. 
Maybe one day, when AI truly sees the world, 
it’ll help us see ourselves a little clearer too.

title: The $5 Trillion Moment
text:
The $5 Trillion Moment 
Nvidia, AI, and the Thin Line Between Confidence and Mania 
The $5 Trillion Moment 
Nvidia, AI, and the Thin Line Between Confidence and Mania 
Three years ago, when ChatGPT first hit the internet, most of us were just playing with it. 
Writing jokes. Asking it for movie scripts. Maybe a bit of code. 
Meanwhile, somewhere in Silicon Valley, Jensen Huang was preparing to change history. 
Yesterday, Nvidia became the first company ever to hit a $5 trillion valuation. 
Five. Trillion. Dollars. 
It’s a number so big it stops meaning anything. Until you realize it’s roughly half the value of every major company in Europe combined. 
And here’s the thing — Nvidia didn’t get here by selling phones or apps or ads. 
It got here by selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush. 
The New Oil 
Every AI startup, every research lab, every tech giant building a model — from OpenAI to Anthropic to Meta — runs on one thing: Nvidia’s chips. 
Without them, the AI revolution wouldn’t just slow down. It would pause. 
That’s why when Huang took the stage in Washington this week, he didn’t sound like a man defending his stock price. 
He sounded like a man defining an era. 
“We have $500 billion in AI chip orders,” he said, brushing off questions about a bubble. 
“I don’t believe we’re in an AI bubble.” 
And maybe he’s right. 
Maybe this isn’t a bubble. Maybe this is what inevitability looks like. 
How We Got Here 
In late 2022, Nvidia was already doing well — but when ChatGPT went viral, something snapped. 
AI became not just a research tool but a religion. 
Companies started pouring billions into GPUs, data centers, and model training. 
The S&P 500 soared, startups rebranded overnight, and suddenly — every problem looked solvable with a neural network. 
Since then, Nvidia’s stock has grown nearly 12x. 
They’re shipping 20 million of their newest chips — five times more than the previous generation. 
Their $500 billion order book doesn’t even count China, thanks to U.S. export bans. 
And while others fight for headlines, Nvidia quietly owns the infrastructure everyone depends on. 
The math is simple: no chips, no AI. 
And Jensen Huang? He sells the chips. 
The Whisper of a Bubble 
Still, history has a sense of humor. 
Every technological leap — from dot-coms to crypto — once sounded “too real to be a bubble.” 
Until it wasn’t. 
Analysts like Matthew Tuttle have started sounding alarms. 
He put it bluntly: “AI’s current expansion relies on a few dominant players financing each other’s capacity.” 
In other words, the AI industry is borrowing tomorrow’s belief to fund today’s hype. 
The moment investors start asking for profits instead of promises, some flywheels could seize. 
And Nvidia? 
It’s standing right in the center of that spinning engine. 
Power, Politics, and Pragmatism 
Huang knows that the future of AI isn’t just built in labs — it’s negotiated in rooms. 
That’s why this week’s GTC keynote in Washington was as much a political theater as a tech showcase. 
He praised Donald Trump for boosting domestic tech investment. 
He warned about isolating China — a market that holds half the world’s AI developers. 
And in his closing line, he nodded to Trump’s old slogan: 
“Thank you for making America great again.” 
It wasn’t a slip. It was strategy. 
Because the next frontier of AI isn’t just about performance — it’s about permission. 
Who gets to build, sell, and scale this technology will shape the next decade of global power. 
Beyond the Numbers 
Behind the headlines and the stock charts, Nvidia’s story is really a story of timing. 
For 20 years, their chips were powering video games and graphics workstations. 
Then, almost overnight, the world realized those same chips were perfect for training AI. 
Huang didn’t invent the revolution — he just showed up ready. 
Now, he’s building seven supercomputers for the U.S. government, powering 100,000 self-driving cars with Uber, and helping Eli Lilly build the world’s most powerful pharma supercomputer. 
It’s hard not to be impressed. 
And yet… it’s equally hard not to feel uneasy. 
When a company becomes bigger than entire markets, when its CEO’s word moves trillions, when its chips decide who wins the AI race — it’s no longer just a company. 
It’s a force. 
The Thin Line Between Confidence and Mania 
Maybe Huang is right. Maybe this isn’t a bubble. 
Maybe this is simply what the future looks like — expensive, accelerated, and inevitable. 
But here’s the uncomfortable truth: 
Every revolution feels rational when you’re inside it. 
Crypto once felt unstoppable. 
The internet boom once felt immortal. 
Today, AI feels inevitable. 
And Nvidia? 
It’s selling the belief that this time is different. 
Maybe it is. 
Or maybe, just maybe, history is waiting to remind us — 
that nothing grows forever, not even the future. 
“Maybe it’s not an AI bubble. Maybe it’s just human belief — inflated to $5 trillion.”

title: The Village That Learned to Think ….Neural Networks Explained Like a Human Story
text:
The Village That Learned to Think ….Neural Networks Explained Like a Human Story 
A magical story that secretly teaches you how neural networks — the brain behind AI — actually work. 
The Village That Learned to Think ….Neural Networks Explained Like a Human Story 
There was once a quiet little village at the edge of a forest. No one knew where it came from or who built it, but everyone agreed on one thing — it was the strangest village they had ever seen. 
This wasn’t a place of farmers or blacksmiths. The people here didn’t grow food or make tools. 
They passed messages. 
Every morning, the villagers would gather in small groups, listen to what others said, do a bit of thinking, and then whisper something new to the next person in line. 
No one person in the village was particularly smart. In fact, most of them didn’t even know what the final goal was. But together, they managed to do something incredible: they could make decisions. 
If someone showed them a picture of a cat or a dog, the villagers would think, whisper, and pass messages until someone at the far end said — 
“I think that’s a cat.” 
The way the villagers worked was both simple and mysterious. 
When one villager spoke to another, they didn’t all speak equally loudly. Some shouted. Some whispered. Some even said the opposite of what they heard. 
Over time, they figured out which voices mattered more. 
If one villager kept giving good clues — say, pointing out whiskers or fur — their words were taken more seriously. If another villager kept leading everyone astray, people learned to tune them out. 
No one told them this rule. It just… evolved. 
Each villager had their own way of reacting to what they heard. Some were cautious — they’d only speak if they were very sure. Others were expressive — blurting out whatever seemed exciting. 
At first, their guesses were terrible. They mistook clouds for sheep, dogs for cats, and once, a bicycle for a bread loaf. But they had a secret. 
Every time they made a mistake, a wise traveler from a nearby city would visit and say, 
“You were off by this much. Now, trace your steps and find out why.” The villagers would whisper backwards, tracing every wrong turn, every misleading voice. Each person made a tiny adjustment in how they listened and spoke the next time. 
They didn’t overhaul their system overnight. They learned in small, careful steps — making their voices just a bit stronger or weaker, adjusting their tone little by little. 
Day after day, season after season, the villagers grew better. 
Soon, they could look at a drawing and say, almost instantly, “That’s a bird,” or “That’s a chair,” or “That’s not anything I’ve seen before.” 
They weren’t born intelligent. They became intelligent by listening, learning, and correcting . 
Years passed. The once-small village grew into a bustling town. More people joined, forming layers of listeners — some focused on tiny details, like edges or shapes, while others thought in patterns, like faces or movements. 
If someone showed them a complex picture, the first few villagers would look only at small features — dots, lines, corners. 
They’d whisper to the next group, who combined those into eyes, noses, and smiles. 
That group would pass their understanding to a few deep thinkers at the end, who’d say confidently, 
“Ah, now I see — this is a human face.” They had unknowingly built a hierarchy of thought. 
Each layer of villagers learned something slightly more complex than the one before. 
One day, the traveler returned again — but this time, he didn’t correct them. 
He simply smiled and said, 
“You’ve done it. You’ve built something that learns.” The villagers looked at one another, confused. 
“Learns?” one of them asked. “We’re just passing whispers.” The traveler chuckled. 
“That’s what all learning really is — passing the right whispers until they make sense.” 
And now, dear reader, let’s finally step back and look at what you’ve been reading. 
That village? 
It wasn’t a real place. 
Each villager was actually a neuron — a tiny mathematical unit. 
Their whispers were numbers . 
Their speaking volume was a weight , controlling how strongly one neuron influenced another. 
The way they reacted — whether they spoke or stayed silent — was called an activation function . 
The wise traveler who corrected them? 
That was backpropagation , the process by which a neural network learns from its mistakes. 
The tiny adjustments each villager made — those were the steps of gradient descent , the way learning happens slowly but surely over time. 
And the many layers of villagers — from the simple listeners to the complex thinkers — formed what we call layers of a neural network . 
At first, they understand nothing. 
But as they see more examples, and the traveler keeps guiding them, the entire system begins to form patterns — just like our village learned what makes a cat a cat. 
This is what happens inside nearly every modern AI system — from your phone’s face unlock to language models that can write essays. 
Millions of artificial “villagers” pass whispers, adjust, and improve until their collective understanding becomes wisdom. 
So next time you hear about an “AI model,” remember: 
it’s not magic, nor mystery — just a village of humble thinkers learning together, one mistake at a time. 
“Intelligence,” said the traveler, “is never born perfect. It is built from whispers — refined through patience, error, and time.”
