title: An AI’s ‘Brain’ Isn’t One Thing
text:
An AI’s ‘Brain’ Isn’t One Thing 
New Research Reveals a Shocking Split Between Memory and Logic 
An AI’s ‘Brain’ Isn’t One Thing 
New Research Reveals a Shocking Split Between Memory and Logic Created by Author We’ve all seen it. You ask an AI chatbot a question, and it recites a perfect, word-for-word quote from a poem. Then, you ask it to solve a simple math problem, and it fails spectacularly. It feels… weird. How can something so “smart” be so “dumb” at the same time? It’s one of the biggest puzzles in artificial intelligence. We treat these giant models like a single “brain,” but what if they’re not? 
New, fascinating research from the AI startup Goodfire.ai suggests that we’ve been looking at it all wrong. In a paper that’s sending ripples through the AI community, researchers have provided the first clear evidence that an AI’s “brain” isn’t one uniform blob of digital neurons. Instead, it has at least two major, completely separate processing features: one for memorization and one for reasoning . 
And the most shocking part? They found a way to surgically separate them. 
The Great Separation: Removing Memory, Keeping Logic 
Think of an AI model like GPT-5. It’s built from “training data,” meaning it has read a massive chunk of the internet, books, and articles. From this, it learns to do two main things: 
Memorize: Recite exact text it has seen before (like a famous quote or a block of code). 
Reason: Apply general principles to solve new problems (like figuring out if a sentence is logical). 
We’ve always assumed these abilities were tangled together. To “reason,” an AI must “remember” the rules of logic, right? 
Wrong. 
The Goodfire.ai researchers discovered that this separation is “remarkably clean.” They found the specific neural pathways responsible for pure memorization. Then, in an experiment that sounds like science fiction, they “removed” those pathways from the model. 
The result? The AI lost 97 percent of its ability to recite training data verbatim. It simply… forgot. But its “logical reasoning” ability? It remained almost completely intact. 
This is a monumental finding. It’s like discovering that in our own brains, the part that remembers your grocery list is in a totally different building from the part that decides what to cook. 
The Twist That Explains Everything: Why AI Fails at Math 
So, if reasoning is separate, where do you think basic math lives? In the logic circuits, right? “2+2=4” is the most basic form of logic. 
This is where the research gets truly wild. The researchers found that basic arithmetic isn’t in the reasoning pathways. It lives in the memorization pathways. 
When they removed the memorization circuits, the AI’s mathematical performance plummeted by 66 percent, even while its logical tasks were untouched. 
Let that sink in. 
This discovery may finally explain why even the most advanced AI language models are notoriously bad at math (without using an external calculator tool). They aren’t “computing” the-answer. They are recalling it. 
As the original article puts it, the AI is “like a student who memorized times tables but never learned how multiplication works.” 
For the AI, “2+2=4” isn’t a logical operation. It’s just a fact it crammed for a test, like “the capital of France is Paris.” If you ask it “2+2,” it searches its memory for that exact fact. If it can’t find it, it tries to guess, often incorrectly. This suggests that at their current scale, these models aren’t “thinking” about numbers at all; they’re just acting like giant, fuzzy lookup tables. 
How Did They Find This? A Trip to the “Loss Landscape” 
To understand how the researchers pulled this off, you need to know about a beautiful concept in AI called the “loss landscape.” 
It’s the key to this whole thing. 
Imagine you’re trying to tune a super-complex machine with millions of dials (these dials are the AI’s “weights”). Your goal is to make the machine get the right answer as often as possible. 
“Loss” is just a measure of how wrong the machine is. High loss = many mistakes. Low loss = few mistakes. 
The “Landscape” is a giant, 3D map showing the “loss” for every possible combination of dial settings. 
When an AI is “training,” it’s essentially “rolling downhill” on this landscape, trying to find the lowest possible valley. That valley is the sweet spot where it makes the fewest mistakes. 
The researchers didn’t just look at the valleys; they analyzed the shape of the landscape, its “curvature.” 
Sharp peaks and deep, narrow valleys have high curvature . A tiny change to a dial sends you flying up or down. 
Flat, open plains have low curvature . You can tweak the dials a lot, and not much changes. 
The Hills of Reasoning vs. The Spikes of Memory 
Here is the “Aha!” moment. The researchers found that reasoning and memorization create completely different shapes in the landscape. 
Reasoning (The Rolling Hills): 
Created by Author General rules — like “if A is taller than B, and B is taller than C, then A is taller than C” — are used by many different inputs. They are shared, robust mechanisms. In the landscape, they look like “consistent moderate curves,” or stable, rolling hills. The researchers write that these directions “add coherently and remain high-curvature on average.” 
Memorization (The Sharp, Hidden Spikes): 
Created by Author A single, specific fact — like a unique quote from a book — is only used for that one input. It creates what the researchers call an “idiosyncratic sharp direction.” It’s a sudden, needle-thin spike in the landscape. 
Here’s the trick: there are millions of these memory-spikes, and they all point in different, random directions. When you average them all out, this spiky, chaotic mess looks… flat. It has a low-curvature profile. 
This was the key. 
The researchers used a technique called K-FAC (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature) to find all the “flat” (low-curvature) parts of the model and all the “hilly” (high-curvature) parts. 
Created by Author They found that the “flat” parts contained all the memorized data. The “hilly” parts contained all the general logic. By removing the low-curvature components, they could erase the memory while leaving the logic-hills perfectly intact. 
What This Means for the Future (and Its Limits) 
This is more than just a cool academic finding. If this technique can be perfected, it could solve some of the biggest problems in AI safety and ethics. 
Imagine an AI model is trained on the whole internet. That means it has memorized private information (like people’s phone numbers or addresses), copyrighted material, and loads of toxic, harmful text. 
Right now, it’s almost impossible to make a model “forget” this bad data without completely retraining it from scratch, which costs millions of dollars. 
This research points to a future where AI companies could “surgically remove” all that sensitive content. You could, in theory, delete all the copyrighted text without breaking the model’s ability to be a useful, creative tool. You could erase the private data without destroying its ability to reason. 
But, we’re not there yet. The researchers are very clear about the limitations. 
It’s Not Perfect: They “cannot guarantee complete elimination of sensitive information.” It’s an early step. 
Memories Can Return: Other research has shown that “forgotten” information can sometimes be reactivated with just a little more training. The data isn’t gone so much as it’s suppressed . 
The “Why” is Still Blurry: We still don’t know why math lives in the memory circuits. Is it truly memorized, or does it just look like memorization to their detection method? 
What’s clear is that we’ve just been given a new map to the hidden, alien landscape of an AI’s mind. For the first time, we’re seeing that it’s not one territory, but at least two. And now, we finally have the tools to start exploring them. 
Credits 
“From Memorization to Reasoning in the Spectrum of Loss Curvature” Reaserach Paper

title: Why Are Lawyers Risking Their Careers for AI?
text:
Why Are Lawyers Risking Their Careers for AI? 
The Real Reason Is Stranger Than You Think. 
Why Are Lawyers Risking Their Careers for AI? 
The Real Reason Is Stranger Than You Think. Created by Author We all have an image of a high-powered lawyer in our heads — think Mike Ross from Suits , someone who knows every case file by heart. 
That’s why it’s one of the strangest puzzles in the professional world right now. 
Real-life lawyers — people who get paid hundreds of dollars an hour to be that meticulous — are suddenly getting caught submitting legal briefs filled with… complete nonsense. 
We’re talking about fake cases, made-up legal precedents, and imaginary facts. 
They’re being sanctioned by furious judges, fined tens of thousands of dollars, and in one case, even fired on the spot by their own client. 
It’s an “epidemic,” according to one judge. But the real mystery isn’t just that they’re getting caught using AI. The truly bizarre part is what happens after they’re caught. 
Instead of just saying “I messed up,” their excuses are getting stranger and stranger. We reviewed the case files, and it turns out these “excuses” are the real story. They reveal what’s actually going on. 
The First Clue: The “I Didn’t Know” Routine 
This is the most common and “innocent” excuse. It’s the “beginner’s mistake,” and it reveals the core technology trap. 
One sanctioned lawyer admitted he didn’t expect ChatGPT to add new fake cases when all he asked it to do was “make his writing more persuasive.” 
Another lawyer in California got hit with a “conservative” $10,000 fine for a similar move. He asked ChatGPT to “enhance” his briefs, then ran them through other AI platforms to “check for errors.” The one step he neglected? Reading the brief himself. 
This is the classic “AI hallucination” problem. The AI isn’t “thinking” or “checking facts.” It’s a hyper-advanced pattern-matcher. (If you’re curious why AI is so good at confidently memorizing but so bad at knowing facts, it’s because it literally has two separate ‘brains’ for memory and reasoning ). It’s been trained on all the legal documents on the internet, and it knows what a legal citation looks like . So, when you ask it to “make it sound more persuasive,” it happily invents a case that looks perfect, right down to the volume number and page. 
It’s like a student who memorized the sound of a history textbook but never learned what the words mean. 
The Second Clue: The “Tech Is Too Hard” Blame Game 
This is where the story gets weirder. After a few lawyers got busted, the “I didn’t know” excuse stopped working. So, the excuses evolved. 
Enter James A. Johnson, an attorney in Alabama. His filing was full of AI-generated lies. His excuse? 
Toggling windows is just too hard. 
He explained to the judge that he was at a hospital with a family member and under time pressure. He had a choice: 
The “Hard” Way: Use Fastcase, the official bar-provided research tool, which “required opening a separate browser.” 
The “Easy” Way: Use a Microsoft Word plug-in called Ghostwriter Legal, which “appeared automatically in the sidebar.” 
He told the court it felt “tedious to toggle back and forth” on his laptop. He fell for the “allure” of the easy button, and it blew up in his face. His own client fired him on the spot. 
Here, the mystery deepens. The lawyer isn’t just blaming ignorance ; he’s blaming inconvenience . The AI didn’t trick him; it was just easier than doing the real work. 
The Final Twist: “My AI Was Hacked!” 
This brings us to the most unbelievable excuse of all — a masterpiece of desperation from a New York lawyer named Innocent Chinweze. 
After being caught, he first admitted to using Microsoft Copilot. But then, he completely changed his story. 
He claimed he had created a draft with correct citations, but then he got HACKED. He told the judge that malicious actors got “unauthorized remote access” to his computer and… meticulously added fake AI citations to his legal brief? 
The judge, as you can imagine, was skeptical, calling it an “incredible and unsupported statement.” 
When this didn’t work, the lawyer “dramatically” changed his story again after lunch, dropping the hacker story and going back to the “I didn’t know it could make things up” excuse. 
So, What’s Really Going On Here? 
This is the “Aha!” moment. The AI isn’t the problem. It’s the catalyst . 
These increasingly bizarre excuses reveal a very human truth: the AI is a shortcut, and these lawyers got caught. But they’re not just getting caught for using AI — they’re getting caught for laziness, arrogance, and a total failure of professional responsibility. 
The AI is just a tool. It’s like a brilliant, lightning-fast, and completely untrustworthy intern. It will write anything you ask, with total confidence. The lawyer’s job is to check its work. 
They didn’t. 
The final irony? Judges say the simplest way to avoid disaster is to just tell the truth. As soon as the error is found, they are begging lawyers to just admit AI was used, act humble, and take a class. 
But some lawyers would rather invent a story about a malicious hacker than admit to the simplest, most embarrassing mistake of all: they didn’t do their homework.

title: The Serial Killer: Why I Trust Data Over Intuition
text:
The Serial Killer: Why I Trust Data Over Intuition 
Most people believe they can spot a monster. 
The Serial Killer: Why I Trust Data Over Intuition 
Most people believe they can spot a monster. Source: Created by Author Free read version 
We think danger announces itself. That it looks suspicious. That it feels wrong in our gut. We trust that some instinct will fire when something truly bad enters the room. 
That belief is comforting. 
It’s also wrong. 
Because in real life, the most dangerous failures don’t look dramatic. They look ordinary. They hide inside routines. They blend into trust. 
Harold Shipman didn’t look like a threat. He looked like a family doctor. He sat in living rooms, drank tea, checked pulses, and reassured worried relatives. He was polite. Familiar. Respected. 
And over years, while no one was watching the pattern , he murdered at least 215 patients. 
Not in a frenzy. Not in bursts. 
Quietly. Methodically. On a schedule. 
Nobody noticed…..not because there was no evidence, but because humans are terrible at noticing slow, cumulative signals. We’re good at reacting to explosions. We’re bad at hearing the ticking. 
That’s why I trust data. 
What Humans Are Bad At Seeing 
Imagine a smoke alarm that only goes off once the house is already on fire. 
That’s how intuition works. 
We notice extremes. We react to headlines. We remember vivid events. But we struggle with gradual change. Ten small deviations feel like nothing. One big deviation feels like everything. 
That’s why a doctor who loses one patient doesn’t raise suspicion. Or two. Or five. Each death has a story. An explanation. A reason that sounds reasonable. 
Humans are storytellers. We connect dots even when they shouldn’t be connected….. and ignore them when they should. 
Data doesn’t do that. 
Data doesn’t care about stories. It only cares about frequencies, baselines, and deviation from expectation. 
The Pattern No One Wanted to See 
David Spiegelhalter, in The Art of Statistics , shows how obvious this becomes once the data is laid out visually. 
Source: The Art of Statistics by David Spiegelhalter 
At first glance, the chart looks almost mundane. Dots scattered across years. Older patients. Nothing that screams “crime scene.” 
But stay with it. 
The bar charts on the edges quietly tell a different story. The ages repeat. The years repeat. The deaths don’t spread out the way chance would suggest. They cluster. Persistently. 
This is what early warning signals often look like in the real world. Not obvious spikes. Just too much consistency where randomness should exist. 
On its own, this visualization is unsettling ….. but still deniable. There’s room for excuses. For stories. 
Then comes the graph that removes that comfort. 
When Noise Turns Into a Signal 
Source: The Art of Statistics by David Spiegelhalter This chart compares the time of day Shipman’s patients died with deaths under other general practitioners. 
For most doctors, the pattern is what you’d expect. A gentle wave. Deaths spread across mornings, evenings, nights. Messy. Human. Random. 
Shipman’s pattern isn’t a wave. 
It’s a spike. 
A sharp, unnatural peak in the early afternoon. Again. And again. And again. 
This isn’t intuition. It isn’t hindsight. It’s a behavioral fingerprint. 
Spiegelhalter notes that this pattern doesn’t require sophisticated statistical analysis. You don’t need equations to feel the wrongness of it. You just need to be willing to look at the distribution instead of the individual stories. 
Thinking in Systems, Not Snapshots 
Most organizations think in snapshots. 
Did anything bad happen today? 
If the answer is no, we move on. 
But harm doesn’t usually arrive all at once. It accumulates. 
Think about credit card fraud. One strange transaction doesn’t shut down your card. But ten slightly strange ones in a row do. 
Or think about a website. A one-second delay once is noise. A one-second delay every day for a month is a problem. 
This is how data scientists think ….. not in isolated events, but in trajectories . 
That’s where the Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) comes in. Not as math trivia, but as a monitoring mindset. 
SPRT doesn’t ask, “Was this event bad?” It asks, “Given everything we’ve seen so far, is this pattern still normal?” 
Each new data point nudges belief slightly. Most of the time, those nudges cancel out. 
But sometimes, they don’t. 
Sometimes the line keeps climbing. 
The Moment the Alarm Should Have Sounded 
Source: The Art of Statistics by David Spiegelhalter This chart tracks how evidence accumulated over time for patients over 64 dying at home or in practice. 
Most lines hover safely between the thresholds. Random variation. Noise. 
But one line ….. tracking Shipman’s female patients ….. keeps rising. 
In 1985 , it crosses the outer alert threshold. 
Not proof. Not a verdict. 
Just a signal saying: 
This pattern is no longer consistent with chance. Shipman wasn’t arrested until 1998. 
In those thirteen years, at least 175 more people died . 
This wasn’t a failure of statistics. The signal was there. 
It was a failure of listening. 
False Alarms Are Not the Enemy 
No real-world monitoring system is perfect. 
Some innocent doctors would have been flagged. Investigations would have happened. Conversations would have been uncomfortable. 
But that’s the cost of early detection. 
Every applied data system makes trade-offs: 
Sensitivity vs. false positives 
Comfort vs. accountability 
Silence vs. scrutiny 
The mistake isn’t triggering an alarm too soon. 
The mistake is never building the alarm at all. 
How This Shapes How I Think About Data 
This story is why I don’t see data as cold or detached. 
To me, data is a safety system. A way to catch slow failures before they become disasters. A way to protect people from our own blind spots. 
I’m drawn to problems where patterns matter more than predictions: 
Monitoring systems 
Anomaly detection 
Risk and churn signals 
Model drift and behavioral change 
I care less about one-off accuracy scores and more about whether a system notices when reality quietly changes. 
Because the most dangerous problems don’t announce themselves. 
They whisper. 
And the job of a data scientist ….. at least the way I see it ….. is to make sure those whispers don’t go unheard. 
Inspired by David Spiegelhalter’s The Art of Statistics

title: Gradient Descent from Scratch
text:
Gradient Descent from Scratch 
By the end, you’ll know not just what gradient descent is …you’ll know how to write it, vectorise it, and use it in production code. 
Gradient Descent from Scratch 
By the end, you’ll know not just what gradient descent is …you’ll know how to write it, vectorise it, and use it in production code. 
Read for free here (if you are not a member) 
Hook 
Every neural network you’ve ever heard of — GPT-4, DALL-E, AlphaFold, the thing that recommends your next YouTube video — learned what it knows through one algorithm. Not a fancy one. Not a secret. One loop that runs over and over, asking a single question: am I going the right direction? 
That’s gradient descent. And it’s genuinely, almost insultingly simple. 
Here’s what most tutorials get wrong: they show you the formula, maybe draw an arrow going downhill, and call it a day. You walk away knowing what gradient descent is, but the moment you open a Jupyter notebook, you’re lost. 
We’re not doing that. By the end, you’ll know not just what gradient descent is — you’ll know how to write it from scratch in raw Python, speed it up with NumPy, and use it in production with PyTorch. Three layers, all connected. 
The Big Picture 
Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm. The goal: given a function, find the input that makes it as small as possible. 
In ML, that function is the loss function — a score measuring how wrong our model’s predictions are right now. The inputs we’re tuning are the model’s parameters (weights, biases — all the numbers the model adjusts during training). Lower loss = better model. Gradient descent is what drives those parameters toward lower loss. 
The ML Training Loop: Data --► Model --► Predictions --► Loss | Compute Gradient | Update Parameters ◄ -- Gradient Descent here | ( repeat until loss plateaus) And this is genuinely what happens inside PyTorch, TensorFlow, and scikit-learn every time you call .fit() or loss.backward() . The libraries handle the bookkeeping, but the core logic is the loop above. 
Real use case: when Google trains its ad ranking model, it has billions of training examples and millions of parameters. A closed-form mathematical solution is impossible at that scale. Gradient descent is the only game in town. 
Intuition Before Math 
Picture a bowl. A regular cereal bowl. Drop a marble into it from the rim. 
The marble doesn’t need a GPS. It doesn’t need a map of the full bowl. It just feels the slope right where it is and rolls downhill. Step by step, it finds the lowest point. 
That’s gradient descent. The bowl is our loss function. The marble is our model’s parameters. The lowest point is the minimum — where the model predicts as accurately as it can. 
Now here’s the part that trips people up: the marble can only feel the slope where it currently is . It can’t see the whole bowl. It takes one small step downhill, checks the slope again, takes another step. This is intentional — in real ML, the “bowl” has millions of dimensions. You can’t solve it globally. You navigate it locally, one step at a time. 
The slope at the marble’s current position is the gradient . It always points in the direction of steepest uphill. So we step in the opposite direction — we subtract the gradient. 
Gradient (Personified): I point uphill. That’s my whole personality. I don’t apologize for it. The one thing our marble gets to control is how far it steps each time. Too large a step and it overshoots the bottom, bounces up the other side, and never settles. Too small and it’ll be rolling forever. 
That step size is the learning rate — the single most finicky number in all of ML. 
Learning Rate (Personified): Set me too high and I’ll blow up your model. Set me too low and your model will still be training when the sun burns out. I am not easy to work with. Now… let’s put some numbers to this. 
The Math — Step by Step 
NERD: What does the gradient actually look like as a number, and how do we use it to take a step? 
Let’s work with f(x) = x² — a bowl-shaped function whose minimum is clearly at x = 0 . Simple enough to trace by hand, exactly the shape of a loss function we'd want to minimize. 
Setup — define everything before we use it: 
f(x) — the function we're minimizing (think: the loss) 
x — our current position (think: one model parameter) 
f'(x) — the derivative of f at x (the gradient, in one dimension) 
α (alpha) — the learning rate, a small constant where 0 < α < 1 
n — number of steps we'll take 
The derivative of f(x) = x²: 
f(x) = x² f '(x) = 2x At any point x , f'(x) is the slope — how steeply the function is climbing right there. Positive means climbing right, negative means climbing left. 
The update rule: 
At each step, we move opposite to the gradient: 
x_new = x_old - α · f '(x_old) = x_old - α · 2 · x_old = x_old · (1 - 2α) Wait, what? Every step just multiplies x by the same constant (1 - 2α) . That means after n steps from a starting point x_0 : 
x_n = x_0 · ( 1 - 2 α)^n For x_n to converge toward zero, we need |1 - 2α| < 1 , which means 0 < α < 1 . Set α ≥ 1 and the multiplier exceeds 1 — each step overshoots by more than it corrects, and x flies off to infinity. The marble launches itself out of the bowl permanently. Let’s verify: x_0 = 5 , α = 0.1 , n = 25 : 
x_25 = 5 · (1 - 0.2)^25 = 5 · (0.8)^25 = 5 · 0.003778... = 0.01889... Twenty-five steps from 5, we’re at 0.019. Closing in on 0. 
A few gotchas before we write code: 
α too high (e.g. 0.6): (1 - 2 · 0.6) = -0.2 , so x alternates sign every step. Still converges, just zigzags like it's having a crisis. 
α ≥ 1 : diverges. The model is cooked. 
Real neural networks: f(x) = x² is a perfect, cooperative bowl. Real loss landscapes have local minima, flat plateaus, and saddle points that make gradient descent genuinely suffer. That's a later episode. 
Okay okay, the NERD is happy. Now let’s actually write this. 
Layer 1 — Pure Python from Scratch 
No libraries. No shortcuts. Just Python and arithmetic so we can see every single operation. 
def gradient_descent_scratch ( init, learning_rate, iterations ): x = init # start at our initial position for step in range (iterations): gradient = 2 * x # f'(x) = 2x - the slope at current x x = x - learning_rate * gradient # x_new = x_old - α · f'(x_old) return x result = gradient_descent_scratch(init= 5.0 , learning_rate= 0.1 , iterations= 25 ) print ( f"After 25 steps: {result: .5 f} " ) # → After 25 steps: 0.01889 The line x = x - learning_rate * gradient IS the update rule from the math. Nothing hidden. 
Sorry (I am not) for the extra verbosity below — but watching it actually descend makes everything click: 
def gradient_descent_verbose ( init, learning_rate, iterations ): x = init print ( f"Step 0: x = {x: .4 f} , f(x) = {x** 2 : .4 f} " ) for step in range ( 1 , iterations + 1 ): gradient = 2 * x x = x - learning_rate * gradient if step <= 5 or step == iterations: print ( f"Step {step:2d} : x = {x: .4 f} , f(x) = {x** 2 : .4 f} " ) gradient_descent_verbose(init= 5.0 , learning_rate= 0.1 , iterations= 25 ) Step 0 : x = 5.0000 , f (x) = 25.0000 Step 1 : x = 4.0000 , f (x) = 16.0000 Step 2 : x = 3.2000 , f (x) = 10.2400 Step 3 : x = 2.5600 , f (x) = 6.5536 Step 4 : x = 2.0480 , f (x) = 4.1943 Step 5 : x = 1.6384 , f (x) = 2.6844 Step 25 : x = 0.0189 , f (x) = 0.0004 Wow. From f(x) = 25 down to f(x) = 0.0004 in 25 steps. 
The catch? This is one parameter. Real models have millions. A Python loop over a million parameters on every training step would take hours. This is where NumPy comes in. 
Layer 2 — NumPy 
Let’s extend the problem: instead of one parameter x , we have a whole vector θ = [θ₁, θ₂, ..., θₙ] . We want to minimize f(θ) = sum(θᵢ²) — same idea, just across all parameters simultaneously. 
In pure Python, that looks like this: 
# Layer 1 extended — pure Python, one element at a time def gd_multi_scratch ( theta_init, learning_rate, iterations ): theta = list (theta_init) for _ in range (iterations): gradients = [ 2 * t for t in theta] # gradient per parameter theta = [t - learning_rate * g for t, g in zip (theta, gradients)] # update each one return theta result = gd_multi_scratch([ 5.0 , - 3.0 , 2.0 ], learning_rate= 0.1 , iterations= 25 ) print ([ round (v, 4 ) for v in result]) # → [0.0189, -0.0113, 0.0076] This works… but looping over a million elements in Python on every step is painful. Here’s the NumPy version: 
import numpy as np # NumPy — Python's numerical computing library, backbone of all ML def gd_multi_numpy ( theta_init, learning_rate, iterations ): theta = np.array(theta_init, dtype= float ) # np.array: wraps a list into a vectorized array for _ in range (iterations): gradient = 2 * theta # operates on ALL elements simultaneously theta = theta - learning_rate * gradient # updates ALL parameters in one line return theta result = gd_multi_numpy([ 5.0 , - 3.0 , 2.0 ], learning_rate= 0.1 , iterations= 25 ) print (np. round (result, 4 )) # → [ 0.0189 -0.0113 0.0076] Same result. The explicit before→after for every change: 
# Layer 1 (pure Python) gradients = [ 2 * t for t in theta] theta = [t - learning_rate * g for t, g in zip(theta, gradients)] # Layer 2 (NumPy) gradient = 2 * theta # one operation, all elements theta = theta - learning_rate * gradient # one operation, all elements Why is NumPy faster? Two reasons. First, it calls compiled C and Fortran code under the hood — no Python interpreter overhead per element. Second, it uses BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), a battle-hardened library of vectorized math routines that CPUs are specifically optimized to run. A million-element update that takes seconds in Python takes milliseconds in NumPy. 
Same result. Way faster. 
Now let’s see what this looks like in the libraries you’d actually use on the job. 
Layer 3 — Production Libraries 
In production, you almost never implement gradient descent yourself. Libraries handle the update step, but also: GPU memory, automatic gradient computation, numerical stability, and fancier variants like Adam and RMSProp. Let’s look at the two tools that matter. 
PyTorch — for deep learning 
import torch # PyTorch — standard library for deep learning research and production import torch.optim as optim # optim: every optimizer lives here — SGD, Adam, RMSProp, all of them # torch.tensor: wraps values in PyTorch's format # requires_grad=True: tells PyTorch to track this variable for gradient computation theta = torch.tensor([ 5.0 , - 3.0 , 2.0 ], requires_grad= True ) # optim.SGD: the packaged version of our update rule - θ = θ - lr · gradient # lr is our learning rate alpha optimizer = optim.SGD([theta], lr= 0.1 ) for step in range ( 25 ): optimizer.zero_grad() # PyTorch accumulates gradients - reset each step loss = (theta ** 2 ). sum () # f(θ) = sum(θᵢ²), same function as Layers 1 and 2 loss.backward() # compute gradients automatically optimizer.step() # apply: θ = θ - lr · gradient print (torch. round (theta.detach(), decimals= 4 )) # → tensor([ 0.0189, -0.0113, 0.0076]) Same result as Layers 1 and 2. Here’s the explicit bridge back: 
loss = (theta * * 2 ). sum () ←→ f(θ) = sum (θᵢ²) [same function , Layer 2 ] loss.backward() ←→ gradient = 2 * theta [we hardcoded this; PyTorch computes it] optimizer.step() ←→ theta = theta - lr * gradient [our update line, Layer 2 ] The big difference is loss.backward() . In Layers 1 and 2 we hardcoded gradient = 2 * theta because we knew the function. In a real neural network with millions of operations chained together, PyTorch computes every gradient automatically. That's the superpower — and the reason it exists. 
scikit-learn — for classical ML 
For linear models (not neural nets), scikit-learn’s SGDRegressor runs gradient descent internally: 
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor # scikit-learn's gradient descent linear model import numpy as np X = np.array([[ 1 ], [ 2 ], [ 3 ], [ 4 ], [ 5 ]], dtype= float ) y = np.array([ 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 ], dtype= float ) # y = 2x model = SGDRegressor(max_iter= 1000 , learning_rate= 'constant' , eta0= 0.01 ) model.fit(X, y) print ( f"Learned weight: {model.coef_[ 0 ]: .4 f} " ) # → Learned weight: 1.9998 SGDRegressor is running our exact loop from Layer 1, applied to minimizing mean squared error on real data instead of x² . The interface hides the loop; the loop is still there. 
When Do You Use Which Layer? 
Reach for pure Python scratch when you’re learning a concept for the first time or debugging something you genuinely don’t understand. If your NumPy implementation produces wrong output and you can’t figure out why, rewrite it in a slow Python loop where you can print() every single value. You'll find the bug in two minutes. Scratch is also the right choice when you need a custom variant no library supports — a weird regularizer, a constrained update, something experimental. 
Reach for NumPy when you’re prototyping or running experiments and need full control over every operation without a full framework’s overhead. NumPy sits in the sweet spot between “slow enough to debug” and “fast enough to be useful.” Most ML research code that isn’t deep learning lives here. 
Reach for PyTorch or scikit-learn when you’re building something real. GPU acceleration, automatic differentiation, and a codebase other people need to read all push you toward the library. For gradient descent specifically: if you’re training a neural network, you’ll always use optim.SGD or optim.Adam . If you're fitting a linear model, SGDRegressor does it. You'd only implement it yourself if you were building a new optimizer variant... or writing a blog post about it. 
Takeaways & What’s Next 
Gradient descent is the loop that runs inside every training algorithm in ML — not optional, load-bearing. Every time you call .fit() , gradient descent is what's running under the hood, taking small steps toward lower loss. The learning rate isn't just a hyperparameter — it's a convergence condition. For f(x) = x² , you need 0 < α < 1 or the whole thing diverges. For real networks, finding a good learning rate is still one of the most consequential (and annoying) parts of the job. The three-layer progression isn't just pedagogy: pure Python shows the mechanics, NumPy shows the scale, PyTorch shows what the industry uses. 
Without gradient descent, linear regression is just a formula you memorize — the closed-form normal equation that works fine on a small dataset and completely falls apart the moment your data has more than a few thousand features. The math breaks down, the matrix inversion becomes impossible, and you’re stuck. Now that you have gradient descent, linear regression becomes something you can actually build and scale. In the next post, we apply this exact update rule to real data: we feed in X and y , compute mean squared error as the loss, and watch a line learn to fit a scatter plot. Every line of code will look familiar — because you wrote the foundation here. 
Try changing the learning rate in the PyTorch example to 1.1 and watch it blow up. That's the convergence condition from the math section, playing out in real code. Drop a comment below if you found a value where it just barely survives. 
See you in Part 2!

title: Building an AI Product From Scratch: Why Detox?
text:
Building an AI Product From Scratch: Why Detox? 
Part: 1 
Building an AI Product From Scratch: Why Detox? 
Part: 1 Before I start talking up a product I’m building, I should say the obvious part out loud: I haven’t built it yet. Not really. What follows isn’t a launch post. It’s the notebook I’m keeping while I figure this out, published before I know whether any of it works. 
read it from here ,if you are not a member. 
So why read about something that isn’t finished? Because if I wrote this after it was done, I’d be tempted to smooth over every wrong turn and make the whole thing sound like it was obvious from the start. Written now, you get the version where I don’t know the ending yet, where the mistakes are still visible instead of edited out afterward. You get two things out of that: something to laugh at when I get it wrong, and something to actually use when I get it right. 
So, why build this at all? 
Where this started 
It starts with my brother watching educational content on YouTube. I was doing my usual “big brother” check to see if he was actually studying, and that’s when I noticed the comment section. The words being used were worrying, and not on some random corner of the internet. This was under education content, the kind kids watch. Which means kids read those comments too, and toxicity like that can affect someone even if they don’t fully understand what it means, maybe especially then. 
It’s not just YouTube, and it’s not just text. It shows up as images. It shows up as text embedded in images, which is worse, because most filters never even look there. And it’s not only a kids’ problem. Plenty of adults would also just prefer a less toxic web to scroll through. 
That’s what I want to fix: a way for toxicity, in whatever form it shows up, to stop being something we just scroll past like it’s normal. 
That’s Detox. 
image created by author 
Is anyone actually solving this 
Before writing a line of code, I looked at what already exists, because building something that already exists well is a waste of everyone’s time. 
There’s a whole category of tools that hide toxic comments, mostly by matching against a keyword list. There’s a separate category for blocking explicit images, usually with decent computer vision behind it but zero understanding of text. There are privacy tools that blur emails and passwords, domain blockers for parental control, and a handful of cloud APIs that big platforms use for moderation at scale. 
Each of these does one narrow thing, and does it in isolation. Most of the capable ones run in the cloud, which means your browsing gets sent somewhere to be scored before you see it. The ones that don’t rely on the cloud are usually just keyword lists, which catch the obvious and miss almost everything else. Nothing I found actually reads a page, understands roughly what it’s looking at, and does that on the device it’s already sitting on. 
That gap is the actual brief: something that runs entirely on the user’s own machine, no API calls, that understands content well enough to flag it instead of just pattern-matching against a list. 
The constraint that rules out the easy path 
That one requirement, run locally, no server calls, decides almost everything else about this project. 
It means I can’t load a big multimodal LLM onto someone’s laptop that might not even have a GPU. Fine, what about a smaller LLM with a tight, efficient prompt? Also no. Even a “small” LLM is still heavy enough that running it on every page someone opens would slow their whole browser down, not just the tab. 
Which means there’s no shortcut here. I can’t wire together whatever’s easiest and call it done. The architecture actually has to be thought through before any of the fun parts start. 
Roughly, how it should work 
Say the extension is built and someone opens a new page. What should happen? 
The page’s text gets pulled out and sent to a model. The model flags whatever looks toxic. The flagged parts get blurred. That’s the whole idea in its simplest form, text only, for now. 
image created by author Simple to say. Then I remember the actual constraint again: no LLM, and no shipping a page’s worth of text off to a server. 
Which means we’re cooked. Well, more accurately, I’m cooked, there’s no “we” here to share the blame with, it’s just me and this laptop. 
That “we’re cooked” turns out to be two separate, both genuinely hard, problems. What model can read a page well enough locally to be worth trusting? And how do you get a page’s text to that model without the whole thing turning into a stuttering mess? 
Picking the model 
Start with the options on the table. 
A purely statistical classifier, something like TF-IDF feeding a simple classifier, is fast in the way that doesn’t always help you. It’s Flash Thompson from the Spider-Man movies: hand shoots up, answer comes out instantly, confidence never wavers, and it’s wrong often enough that you learn not to fully trust it. No real sense of what a sentence means once the wording gets even a little clever. 
A full LLM is the opposite problem. It genuinely understands nuance and catches what a keyword list never would, closer to Doctor Strange running through those fourteen million futures before he says a word. Correct, eventually. But you did not just casually run fourteen million simulations to answer one question, and neither can someone’s laptop, for every sentence, on every page, all day. 
Like a wise person definitely told me at some point, life isn’t black and white, it’s more like fifty shades of grey (kidding, mostly). There’s a middle ground here, and it’s a small transformer, not a full LLM, just the architecture underneath one, trained for exactly one narrow job instead of everything at once. Light enough that I can actually train it without a research budget. Light enough to run on a normal laptop. Still able to read a sentence in context instead of just matching it against a list of banned words. 
That’s the model. Whether it’s good enough is a problem for the next post. 
image created by author 
One problem already solved, one still open 
Getting text to the model efficiently isn’t a new problem, so I don’t have to solve it from nothing. Batches, not single sentences: collect the text on a page, send it over in groups, get classifications back for the group. That part just needs implementing carefully, not inventing. 
The part I don’t have an answer for yet: toxicity isn’t one thing. There are different types and different severities, and blurring every flagged sentence the exact same way flattens all of that into a single blunt signal. My current best guess is that the fix lives in the interface, not the model. Different categories of flagged content could read differently, maybe through color, maybe through how strongly something is blurred, so a reader gets a sense of what they’re choosing to reveal before they click. That’s a real open question, not a solved one, and I’d rather say that plainly than pretend I’ve already figured it out. 
What’s next 
That’s roughly the shape of it: extract the text, batch it, classify it locally, blur what’s flagged, and figure out an interface that doesn’t reduce every kind of harm to the same gray smudge. 
The next post is the part I’ve been putting off writing about, because it’s the part I actually have to go build: training the transformer itself, on real data, and finding out how wrong my assumptions above turn out to be. If you want to follow along, including the parts that don’t work, the repo’s public.

title: Reinforcement learning : Zero to Hero to God
text:
Reinforcement learning : Zero to Hero to God 
one of the most advanced topics in AI made easy and exciting 
Reinforcement learning : Zero to Hero to God 
one of the most advanced topics in AI made easy and exciting 
Explain why RL is important (and how advanced it is) 
and how it basically mimics the Human behavior in real life world where Humans learn based on experience 
Explain the structure of this course 
Phase 1: The Mathematical Bedrock (Zero) 
Focus: Understanding the Agent-Environment loop without the noise of Deep Learning. 
Blog Topics (Theory): 
The RL Framework: Agents, Environments, State ($S$), Action ($A$), Reward ($R$). 
Markov Decision Processes (MDPs): The Markov Property, Trajectories, and Discount Factors ($\gamma$). 
The Bellman Equations: The heart of RL. Deriving $V(s)$ (Value Function) and $Q(s, a)$ (Action-Value Function). 
Dynamic Programming: Policy Iteration vs. Value Iteration. 
Visual: 
Image of Reinforcement Learning Agent Environment Loop 
Getty Images 
Explore 
Kaggle Notebooks (Practice): 
Notebook 1: Solving FrozenLake from Scratch. Implement the Bellman updates manually using Python dictionaries (no Neural Networks yet). 
Notebook 2: Monte Carlo vs. Temporal Difference (TD). Implementing Q-Learning and SARSA on Taxi-v3 . 
Phase 2: Value-Based Deep RL (The Bridge) 
Focus: Replacing “Lookup Tables” with Neural Networks. 
Blog Topics (Theory): 
The Curse of Dimensionality: Why tables fail in complex worlds (e.g., Images). 
Deep Q-Networks (DQN): The 2015 DeepMind breakthrough. 
Stability Tricks: Experience Replay Buffers and Target Networks. 
The “Rainbow” Improvements: Double DQN, Dueling Architectures, and Prioritized Experience Replay (PER). 
Kaggle Notebooks (Practice): 
Notebook 3: DQN on CartPole. Build a DQN using PyTorch/TensorFlow. Focus on the “Training Loop.” 
Notebook 4: Mastering Atari (Pong/Breakout). Implementing CNN-based DQN. 
Tip: Use CleanRL implementations here for readability, then Stable Baselines3 to show production-grade code. 
Phase 3: Policy Gradients & Continuous Control (Hero) 
Focus: Handling robotics and environments where actions are not just “Left/Right” but continuous values. 
Blog Topics (Theory): 
Policy Gradients (PG): The REINFORCE algorithm and the Log-Derivative trick. 
The Variance Problem: Why PG is noisy and how “Baselines” fix it. 
Actor-Critic Methods: Combining Value (Critic) and Policy (Actor) learning (A2C/A3C). 
Kaggle Notebooks (Practice): 
Notebook 5: REINFORCE on LunarLander. 
Notebook 6: Actor-Critic on Acrobot. Visualize how the Critic reduces the variance of the Actor. 
Phase 4: State-of-the-Art Algorithms (Elite) 
Focus: The algorithms actually used in the industry today (OpenAI, DeepMind). 
Blog Topics (Theory): 
PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization): The industry standard. Explain “Clipping” and “Trust Regions” simply. 
Visual: 
Off-Policy Wizards: DDPG (Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient) and TD3. 
SAC (Soft Actor-Critic): Adding “Entropy” to encourage exploration. This is crucial for modern robotics. 
Kaggle Notebooks (Practice): 
Notebook 7: PPO on BipedalWalker (Hard Mode). 
Notebook 8: SAC on Humanoid (MuJoCo/PyBullet). Show how SAC explores better than PPO. 
Phase 5: The Frontier (God Mode) 
Focus: Generative AI, LLMs, and Offline RL. This makes your course “Elite.” 
Blog Topics (Theory): 
Model-Based RL: DreamerV3 and World Models. Learning a model of the world to “dream” future states. 
Offline RL: Learning from static datasets without interacting with the environment (Conservative Q-Learning). 
RLHF (RL from Human Feedback): How ChatGPT uses PPO to align language models. 
Decision Transformers: Treating RL as a sequence modeling problem (like GPT). 
Kaggle Notebooks (Practice): 
Notebook 9: Offline RL with d3rlpy. Train an agent using only a saved dataset of replays. 
Notebook 10: Mini-RLHF. Fine-tune a small Language Model (e.g., GPT-2 or TinyLlama) to output positive sentiments using a Reward Model and PPO (use the trl library from Hugging Face).
